concepts.summary: Aluminium ions from alum or aluminium acetate deposited on cotton coordinate with hydroxy-anthraquinone dyes to form an insoluble coloured complex fixed to the fibre, so colour develops only where the mordant was printed.
concepts.body_md:
A mordant is a metal salt that forms an insoluble complex with dye molecules; mordants are key to the fastness of natural dyes on cotton. In Indian printing, alum paste is applied only to selected areas, and in the subsequent red dye bath the dye is fixed there. Solid-state 27Al NMR of re-created (oiled and alumed) Turkey red calico shows aluminium in six-fold coordination with oxygen ligands (-OH, COO- or both).

*Simplification:* exactly how Al3+ anchors to cellulose is not settled. In the Turkey red process studied by Wertz, aluminium is held largely as fatty-acid carboxylates from the oil; Indian block printing uses no comparable oiling. That tannin pre-treatment plays an analogous anchoring role in Indian practice is an inference from the general statement that tannins chelate metals and attract more mordant; it is not demonstrated in the cited sources. A direct Al-cellulose bond should not be presented as established.

concepts.summary: Hydroxy-anthraquinone dyes such as alizarin chelate aluminium (with calcium) to form an insoluble red lake. Where iron is printed instead, the same red bath gives black or dark purple; whether that colour is an iron-dye lake, an iron-tannate, or both is unresolved.
concepts.body_md:
The red of Turkey red is a lake of alizarin, aluminium and calcium; alizarin can form six-member chelate rings with aluminium ions, and the large insoluble complex is likely also physically trapped in the fibre. Strong-acid extraction probably releases the dye by replacing the metal with protons.

In Indian mordant printing a single red dye bath develops red on alum-printed areas and black or dark purple on iron-printed areas.

*Simplifications:* (1) The proposed Ca-Al-alizarin structures (Kiel & Heertjes; Soubayrol et al.) come from European Turkey red and alizarin studies, and the S1 mechanism statements come from work on hair fibres. (2) Indian red dyes include *Morinda citrifolia* (Al), *Rubia cordifolia* (munjeet) and chay root (*Oldenlandia umbellata*), which are chemically different from dyer's madder; today synthetic alizarin is common. (3) The cited sources do not document the coordination chemistry of the iron dark colour. The colour outcome is documented; the mechanism is only inferred by analogy (see open question).

concepts.summary: Iron salts (in India, iron acetate from fermented scrap iron) react with tannins on the cloth to give black, grey or brown; the same system is acidic and iron-catalysed, and progressively weakens cotton ('iron rot').
concepts.body_md:
Iron mordants combined with tannins give deep blacks, greys and browns. With hydrolysable tannins, ferrous iron forms blue-black iron(III)-tannate complexes whose colour arises from charge transfer across the Fe(III)-O bond. In Indian printing the iron liquor is iron acetate made from fermented scrap iron; printed on myrobalan-treated cloth it gives dark outlines and fields.

The same chemistry is a known conservation problem. Iron-tannate dyeing makes cotton acidic, and acid hydrolysis plus iron-catalysed oxidation weaken and embrittle the fibre, as iron-gall ink corrodes paper. In controlled studies, model iron-tannate-dyed cotton had a surface pH of about 2.7-3.9 against 5.4-7.5 for undyed cloth (Wilson et al.), or an extract pH of 4.08 against 6.85 (Redzic et al.). Under accelerated ageing it lost tensile strength faster and more than undyed controls. On a Met Indian block-printed fragment, the iron-acetate/myrobalan areas show fibre loss.

*Simplification:* the laboratory evidence uses ferrous sulfate (or another iron salt) with tannic acid, not traditional iron acetate and myrobalan. Accelerated ageing may also weight the two degradation routes differently from natural ageing.

concepts.summary: Water-insoluble indigo is reduced in an alkaline, oxygen-poor vat to soluble leuco-indigo, which penetrates the fibre and re-oxidises to insoluble blue indigo when the cloth is lifted into air.
concepts.body_md:
Indigo is not water-soluble; leuco-indigo is. Reduction is carried out either by indigo-reducing bacteria in a fermentation vat or chemically (sodium dithionite). Traditional fermentation vats are anaerobic and strongly alkaline, kept above about pH 10.3-10.5 with slaked lime. Cloth dipped in the vat takes up leuco-indigo, and brief exposure to air oxidises it back to insoluble blue indigo on the fibre.

*Simplification:* the microbiology cited is from Japanese sukumo vats; the organisms, reductants and pH of Indian vats are not documented in these sources. That repeated dips deepen the shade is common craft knowledge, but no source here documents it.

concepts.summary: A printed paste of clay or silt, lime and natural gum dries into a coating that keeps dye liquor from the fibre beneath. Where the dried paste cracks, dye seeps through and leaves fine crackle lines. This is a descriptive reading; no physico-chemical study of Dabu was found.
concepts.body_md:
Dabu-type resists are pastes of clay or river silt with lime and a natural gum (one documented recipe adds sugar-cane molasses). The paste is printed on areas meant to stay undyed, often sprinkled with sawdust, and sun-dried until hard before dip dyeing. Descriptions call the dried paste impermeable, and say dye penetrating cracks in the resist produces characteristic crack lines.

*Physical analogue (not Dabu-specific):* in laboratory work, drying clay films crack only above a critical thickness. Crack spacing is roughly the film thickness, and thicker layers give fewer, wider cracks; composition, drying rate, humidity and substrate all change the pattern. This suggests why crackle depends on paste thickness and drying, but it was measured for pure bentonite on glass, not for silt-lime-gum paste on cotton.

*Gap:* no peer-reviewed analysis of Dabu was found, whether of mineralogy, porosity, the roles of lime, gum and molasses, or why the dried paste withstands the indigo vat. The barrier mechanism is inferred from museum and archive descriptions. Hence needs_evidence.

concepts.summary: Cotton is first treated with tannin-rich myrobalan. Tannins are metal-chelating polyphenols, said to help the cloth take up more mordant; for aluminium this is described as probable, not demonstrated. With iron, tannin itself forms the black.
concepts.body_md:
Most natural dyes have low affinity for cellulose compared with protein fibres. Before mordant printing, Indian cotton is soaked in myrobalan (harde), a fruit rich in hydrolysable tannins. Tannins are polyphenols with many -OH groups that chelate metals. Dyers knew they improved colour uptake by attracting more mordant, and they probably acted as a secondary mordant by attracting aluminium. Cellulose can hold tannic acid by hydrogen bonding and can also bind metal ions. With iron, tannin itself forms the black (see iron-tannin-black).

*Simplification:* the cited thesis gives tannin-aluminium bridging as probable, not demonstrated, and its context is European Turkey red. No quantitative study of myrobalan as a cotton pre-mordant was found.

concepts.summary: Wet cloth spread in sunlight between treatments whitens the unmordanted ground. Museum sources attribute this to oxidation, consistent with the photo-oxidative mechanism known from light bleaching of cellulose (paper), but it has not been studied for Indian practice.
concepts.body_md:
Indian printers repeatedly lay cloth in the sun during cleaning and between dyeing stages. The Met describes this as bleaching by oxidation, and chintz process documents describe washing and bleaching between colours. A reconstruction treated ample sunlight as a fixed requirement of the bleaching and substituted full-spectrum lamps.

*Closest studied analogue:* aqueous light bleaching of paper (cellulose) by sunlight or lamps. There, a coloured impurity (chromophore) absorbs light and is converted to a reactive peroxide or free radical, which oxidises chromophores to colourless products that may wash out. Light can also degrade the substrate. Conservation work on cotton confirms that discolouration can be lessened by oxidative bleaching and that bleaching generally damages fibres.

*Gap:* no fetched study characterises traditional sun bleaching of cotton cloth. It is unknown which species form, whether dung or alkali residues matter, and how stray dye is cleared from the ground. The mechanism is given only at the level of photo-oxidative whitening by analogy and marked needs_evidence.

concepts.summary: Thickeners such as natural gums set a print paste's viscosity and flow; this controls how far the paste spreads and penetrates, and hence the sharpness of the printed mark.
concepts.body_md:
In textile printing, sharpness, penetration, colour yield and retention of white ground depend heavily on paste viscosity and rheology, and viscosity depends on the thickener. Low-viscosity paste spreads and penetrates deeply. Pseudoplastic (shear-thinning) pastes such as guar gum become less viscous as shear rate increases. Indian resist pastes include natural gum.

*Simplification:* evidence is from modern reactive-dye screen printing. No measured rheology of traditional block-printing mordant or Dabu pastes was found, and the thickeners of Indian mordant pastes are not documented in this file. Apply as an analogy only.

concepts.summary: Starch size from weaving and natural waxes, fats and pectins make grey cotton water-repellent; removing them makes the cloth absorbent and receptive to mordants and dyes.
concepts.body_md:
Warp yarns are coated with a size, most often starch, to survive weaving, and it must be removed before dyeing (desizing). Raw cotton also carries hydrophobic impurities in the cuticle (waxes, fats) and primary wall (pectin, proteins, organic acids), which scouring removes. In Indian block printing, cloth is cleaned with a camel-dung, castor-oil and soda-ash solution, trampled and beaten, and laid in the sun repeatedly.

*Simplification:* these sources do not analyse the chemistry of the traditional dung, castor-oil and soda wash (for example soap formation or enzymatic action of dung).

concepts.summary: Aluminium salt used as the red-producing mordant; historically potassium aluminium sulfate, sometimes converted to aluminium acetate for cellulose.
concepts.body_md: Alum is potassium aluminium sulfate. In European practice it was also converted to aluminium acetate ('red liquor'), considered better for cellulosic fibres. In India alum is printed as a paste to localise red.

concepts.summary: Iron mordant liquor made by fermenting scrap iron; gives black with tannins and dark shades under red dyes, and is corrosive to cotton.
concepts.body_md: In Indian printing the iron mordant is iron acetate prepared from fermented scrap iron. Recipes (jaggery, vinegar, fermentation time) belong in tradition files. The ferrous/ferric balance of the traditional liquor is not documented here.

concepts.summary: Hydroxy-anthraquinone red dyes from Rubiaceae roots (Indian: Morinda citrifolia/Al, Rubia cordifolia/munjeet, chay root) or synthetic alizarin.
concepts.body_md: Traditional Indian reds come from several Rubiaceae plants that differ chemically from European dyer's madder; most artisans now use synthetic alizarin.

concepts.summary: Water-insoluble blue vat dye (natural from Indigofera, or synthetic) applied via its reduced leuco form.
concepts.body_md: Indigo from Indigofera tinctoria, increasingly replaced by synthetic indigo, is applied by vat reduction.

concepts.summary: Tannin-rich fruit used as cotton pre-treatment; its tannins are predominantly hydrolysable (gallotannins, ellagitannins, chebulagic/chebulinic acids).
concepts.body_md: About 60 tannin compounds have been reported in myrobalan fruit, predominantly hydrolysable tannins. When the fruit is sun-dried these degrade to gallic, ellagic and chebulic acids, so the tannin profile of a dye-bath extract depends on how the fruit was processed (not studied for dyeing).

concepts.summary: Cellulose fibre substrate of all six traditions; low natural affinity for most natural dyes and susceptible to acid/iron and oxidative damage.
concepts.body_md: Cotton is cellulose with surface waxes, fats and pectins; most natural dyes have poor affinity for it without mordants.

concepts.summary: Plant gums (locally gond; e.g., gum arabic, guar) used to thicken mordant and resist pastes.
concepts.body_md: Natural gums appear in resist pastes; guar is a galactomannan giving pseudoplastic pastes. Specific gums used per tradition should be sourced in tradition files.

concepts.summary: Alkali used to keep indigo fermentation vats at high pH and as an ingredient of mud-resist paste.
concepts.body_md: Slaked lime maintains vat alkalinity; it is also listed in Dabu paste recipes.

concepts.summary: Fine mineral sediment forming the body of mud-resist pastes.
concepts.body_md: River-bed silt or clay forms the bulk of Dabu paste.

concepts.summary: Red developed on alum-mordanted areas in a madder-family or alizarin bath.
concepts.body_md: Red appears only where alum was applied; unmordanted ground is washed or bleached clear.

concepts.summary: Black, grey, brown or dark purple developed where iron mordant meets tannin (and red dye).
concepts.body_md: Used for outlines and dark fields; associated with long-term fibre loss.

concepts.summary: Insoluble blue indigo fixed on the fibre after vat dyeing and air oxidation.
concepts.body_md: Blue indigo is deposited on the fibre when leuco-indigo picked up in the vat re-oxidises in air.

concepts.summary: Fine dyed veins where dye penetrated cracks in dried mud resist.
concepts.body_md: A visual signature of mud-resist printing.

concepts.summary: Sources document black or dark purple where iron is printed before a red dye bath, but do not resolve whether this is an iron-anthraquinone lake, an iron-tannate from the myrobalan ground, or both.
concepts.body_md: Both iron-tannin and iron-dye complexes are plausible on myrobalan-treated cloth dyed in Rubiaceae baths; no fetched source separates the contributions.

concepts.summary: Which photo-oxidative reactions whiten the ground and clear loosely held dye during repeated sun exposure, and at what cost to fibre strength, is not characterised for Indian practice.
concepts.body_md: Museum sources attribute the whitening to oxidation. Light bleaching of wet paper proceeds through photo-generated peroxides or radicals that oxidise chromophores, and oxidative bleaching damages cotton. No direct study of field sun bleaching of cotton was found.

concepts.summary: Clay-based resist pastes are documented for Ajrakh (gach), Dabu, Bagru and Sanganeri; Ajrakh and Dabu also use lime for fine outlines; wax resist appears only in a general kalamkari account, not a Pedana-specific one.
concepts.body_md: Every clay resist in the dataset is printed before indigo and washed off afterwards. The pastes share clay, gum and lime or a cereal filler, and are dusted while wet. They differ in role: Ajrakh gach carries alum, so it resists indigo and later mordants the red, whereas the Rajasthani dabu is a pure resist used only for indigo patterns. Dabu sources record resists graded by strength. Wax for Machilipatnam rests on a general kalamkari description and an undated raw-material list.

concepts.summary: In Ajrakh, Dabu, Bagru and Sanganeri, indigo is a vat dip around a printed resist; at Machilipatnam the documented practice prints indigo directly because it needs no mordant.
concepts.body_md: The dip traditions share the folded-cloth dip, green-to-blue oxidation and depth built by repeated dips, with the vat judged by experience. Ajrakh dyers are reported to taste the vat; Bagru and Sanganeri dyers read its colour.

concepts.summary: Ajrakh, Bagh, Bagru, Sanganeri and Machilipatnam kalamkari all pre-treat cotton with myrobalan, print alum for red and fermented iron for black, then develop colour in a red bath; Dabu sources document this only for Bagru.
concepts.body_md: The shared chain is: myrobalan (tannin) pre-treatment → iron and alum mordant printing → curing → washing out unfixed mordant → one red bath giving red on alum and black on iron. Differences worth comparing: in Ajrakh the iron black is said to develop on printing from the tannin, while Bagh sources describe the black forming in the alizarin bath; Ajrakh inserts the clay-resist and indigo stages between mordant printing and the red bath; and practitioners in Ajrakh and Machilipatnam keep lime or iron away from alum. Iron liquor is fermented scrap iron with jaggery everywhere; Bagh sources also describe market ferrous sulphate.

concepts.summary: Sources record madder (Ajrakh, Bagru, Sanganeri), aal root (Bagh) and chay or madder (Machilipatnam) as earlier reds, now largely synthetic alizarin; Akola Dabu moved from alizarin to naphthol. Each red bath adds a local plant.
concepts.body_md: Alizarin replaces a root dye in every mordant tradition; the alum mordant stays. Akola Dabu is the exception: its red is now a naphthol printed and developed with "red salt", which needs no alum-and-boil bath. Red-bath additives differ by plant and stated role: tamarisk added when colour spreads (Ajrakh), dhawai/dhavda flowers to avoid patches or for shine and fixing (Bagru, Sanganeri, Bagh), and jajaku/gaja leaves as carrier or fixer (Machilipatnam). Bath times recorded: up to four hours (Ajrakh), about three or five to six hours (Bagh), half a day (Bagru, Sanganeri), about 1.5 hours (Machilipatnam).

concepts.summary: The red bath tints unmordanted cloth; Ajrakh, Sanganeri and Bagh clear it with dung, water and sun, Bagru leaves an off-white ground, and Machilipatnam sources describe a pinkish ground.
concepts.body_md: This is a process-to-outcome chain that differs between traditions: an extra clearing stage (tapano, tapai, tarai) produces a white ground; its absence leaves cream or pink. Both GI texts that explain clearing credit dung and sun; this is not chemically studied (shared sun-bleaching mechanism is needs_evidence).

concepts.summary: Recorded lengths differ widely: Ajrakh 14–16 stages over 15–21 days; Bagh at least three weeks after printing; Machilipatnam up to almost two months; Bagru and Sanganeri ageing of at least three to four days; Dabu is cyclic, one resist-and-dye round per colour.
concepts.body_md: Durations are not measured on a common basis and the stage counts in the files reflect how each source divides the work. The comparison is safest at the level of shared stage types: repeated scouring with oil and dung, a curing or ageing rest after mordant printing, and washing out unfixed mordant before the red bath.

concepts.summary: All six traditions depend on flowing water for washing; four attribute colour quality to local water without measurements, Ajrakh sources instead report iron in water as harmful, and several record falling water and effluent pollution.
concepts.body_md: Comparable structure across files: a river that drew printers to the site, a claim that the water improves colour (untested), a later water crisis, and pollution attributed mainly to chemical or screen printing. The Ajrakh iron case is the one place where a specific water constituent is linked to a colour defect, and a Bagh source credits iron with the opposite effect.

concepts.summary: Bagru, Sanganeri and Akola Dabu sources name Chhipa printers (Bagru and Sanganer accounts link them to Sant Namdev); Ajrakh and Bagh sources name Khatris from Sindh who migrated about 400 years ago. The labels overlap.
concepts.body_md: The Khatri accounts (Ajrakh, Bagh) share a Sindh origin. The Chhipa accounts (Bagru, Sanganer) trace movement within Rajasthan or from Gujarat. The labels are not exclusive: the Bagh GI calls the Khatris a community of chhipas; Bagru and Sanganer survey respondents were mostly Khatri or Chhipa; Sanganer screen printing came with Khatri migrants from Sind; and one craft organisation credits Dabu to Khatris while Akola sources name Chhipas. Machilipatnam has a different, multi-caste karkhana organisation.

concepts.summary: Ajrakh, Bagh, Bagru, Dabu and Sanganeri sources all record designs, colours or cloth formats reserved for particular client communities, with much of that differentiation now gone.
concepts.body_md: This is a shared relational pattern (community → design and colour choice) present in five files, useful as a cross-tradition link that does not depend on dye chemistry. Some communities recur: Jat appears in Ajrakh, Bagh, Bagru and Dabu sources.

concepts.summary: Registry records show five registered GIs (Machilipatnam Kalamkari 2008, Bagh Prints 2008, Sanganeri 2009-10, Bagru 2011, Kutch Ajrakh 2024) and one pending application (Aakola Dabu, Pre Examination); secondary sources misreport several dates.
concepts.body_md: GI status is a historical attribute, not craft knowledge, but it matters for source quality: GI journal texts are applicant-written and supply much of the process content. Screen-printed imitation is cited as a motive for the Bagru and Sanganeri applications, and a 2025 study found the GI rarely used in marketing at either centre.

concepts.summary: The Bagru and Sanganeri files describe the same mordant, dabu, indigo, yellow and alum stages in near-identical words; the documented process difference is Sanganer's sun-bleaching (tapai), which gives a white rather than cream ground.
concepts.body_md: For a study, these two traditions would test almost the same causal chain twice. Their shared descriptions come from GI applicant texts that are nearly word-for-word the same, so the parallel is partly an artefact of a single boilerplate source.

concepts.summary: A multi-stage resist and mordant block-printing and dyeing tradition of the Khatri community, practised in Kutch (Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka, Khavda), Barmer and Sindh, registered as the GI 'Kutch Ajrakh' (application 1050).
concepts.body_md: Kutch Ajrakh is described in its GI specification as an elaborate resist block-printing technique combining direct and resist printing with dyeing, using natural dyes and hand-carved wooden blocks. Traditionally the palette is blue, red, black and white. The process and designs are shared by Sindh, Kutch and Barmer, and the printers are Khatri artisans whose ancestors came from Sindh.

concepts.summary: Sources place Ajrakh's origin in Sindh, at the Indus delta, and link it to the deep history of dyed and printed cotton in the Indus region.
concepts.body_md: The 1971 Kutch Gazetteer (quoted in the GI journal) states Ajrakh printing originally came from Sindh. The GI text and Khamir both invoke Indus Valley evidence of dyeing, but the link between Harappan finds and Ajrakh specifically is interpretive.

concepts.summary: Khatri printers from Sindh settled in Kutch, commonly said to be at the invitation of the ruler of Kutch (Rao Bharmalji I), who granted land and tax concessions; the date is disputed.
concepts.body_md: The GI text says the technique came to Kutch about 400 years ago at the invitation of the King of Kutch, who invited Khatris to practise on the Dhamadka river banks. Sahapedia names Rao Bharmalji I (1586-1631). Khamir records oral histories of a 7th-century flight from Sindh and a lineage from Jinda Jeeva arriving around 1650.

concepts.summary: Dhamadka village in Kutch, on a river that supplied the printers' water, was the main Ajrakh centre for centuries before 2001.
concepts.body_md: The GI journal says Ajrakh activity prevailed at Dhamadka for about 450 years because of a water source from a stream of the Indus; the rangchulis lay around the old river (Khamir describes rangchulis as boiling/dyeing pots at the river's edge). The stream dried in 1989. Khamir names the river Saran.

concepts.summary: After the 2001 Kutch earthquake devastated Dhamadka and worsened its water, Khatri printers relocated about 40 km and founded Ajrakhpur, a village built for printers.
concepts.body_md: Sources agree that the 2001 earthquake triggered relocation from Dhamadka to the new settlement of Ajrakhpur, chosen partly for its water. Family counts differ (about 80 per Khamir; over 100 per GI and Mongabay).

concepts.summary: Ajrakh was traditionally made for Maldhari pastoralists and other local communities, used as turbans, lungis, shoulder cloths and bundles, with community-specific designs.
concepts.body_md: Khatris did not wear the cloth themselves but printed for Maldhari and farming communities, often bartering for produce. Each client group had distinct palettes and designs that printers kept consistent.

concepts.summary: Synthetic alizarin and indigo largely displaced natural madder and indigo; a revival of natural dyeing has occurred, with many printers now working with both.
concepts.body_md: The GI journal notes synthetic alizarin (1868) rapidly superseded madder, whose use almost disappeared until a recent revival. Khamir dates the wider chemical-dye shift to the early 1950s and a craft revival to the 1970s.

concepts.summary: Ajrakh was worn on both sides of the Indus before Partition; the 1947 border closed trade between Kutch and Sindh.
concepts.body_md: Sahapedia notes ajrakh was worn by Sindhi Muslim animal-keepers across Sindh, Kutch and Marwar before Partition; Khamir records the collapse of East Kachchh-Sindh trade in 1947. In Sindh ajrak remains a symbol of cultural identity.

concepts.summary: Medieval Gujarati resist-printed cotton fragments found at Fustat (Egypt) are cited as resembling Ajrakh-type designs.
concepts.body_md: Dua cites 15th-century resist-printed fragments from Gujarat found at Fustat; Khamir says Al Fustat block-prints (11th-14th c.) resemble designs still printed in Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur.

concepts.summary: Barmer is a secondary Ajrakh centre; Sahapedia reports a sharp decline from 40-50 Khatri families in the 1970s to five or six part-time.
concepts.body_md: Sahapedia's Barmer interviews report family numbers falling; the GI text notes Barmer ajrakh has a narrower design range than Kutch.

concepts.summary: The Ajarakhpur Hastkala Vikas Sangathan filed for the 'Kutch Ajrakh' GI in January 2023, facilitated by the Textiles Committee; it was registered in 2024.
concepts.body_md: The GI covers classes 24 and 25 and names Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda as the villages maintaining the tradition. The inspection body includes the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts), the Textiles Committee, GSHHDC, two master artisans and the applicant.

concepts.summary: Iron in the water supply dulls and darkens Ajrakh and produces black spots on myrobalan-treated cloth; rising iron is cited as a reason for leaving Dhamadka and a renewed threat at Ajrakhpur.
concepts.body_md: The GI method says water rich in alum, tin or chrome brightens colours while iron dulls and darkens the result. Artisans quoted by Mongabay describe black spots on harde-treated cloth when iron is present; Khamir records that iron rose sharply after the earthquake, making off-white grounds impossible.

concepts.summary: Ajrakh is very water-intensive; falling water tables and salinity threaten production, and an effluent treatment plant now recycles water at Ajrakhpur.
concepts.body_md: Mongabay reports about 1 lakh litres used per day and a NITRA-built CETP with iron filtration; Frater notes an effluent system built in 2022. Khamir reports the water level at Ajrakhpur falling 10-15 feet a year.

concepts.summary: Historically Ajrakh printing concentrated where very soft water was available.
concepts.body_md: The 1971 Kutch Gazetteer, quoted in the GI journal, says Ajrakh 'got concentrated where extra soft water was available'. A Khavda printer quoted by Khamir says dyeing methods were the same as elsewhere but local water and weather changed the shades.

concepts.summary: Sun-drying follows most stages, and stage timing is tied to time of day: outlines in the morning, iron black in the afternoon, mud resist late in the day, final wash in cool early morning.
concepts.body_md: The GI method repeatedly specifies sun-drying and time-of-day preferences, and explains that warm afternoon water may dissolve alum.

concepts.summary: Humidity slows production and affects natural dyes; blocks are oiled to prevent swelling in the rainy season.
concepts.body_md: Khamir notes monsoon humidity slows production and stops natural dyes reaching full effect; the GI text says blocks are soaked in mustard oil so they do not expand in the rains.

concepts.summary: Ajrakh is printed mainly on market-bought cotton of 60s-120s count; silk is used for custom orders.
concepts.body_md: Earlier, narrow pit-loom cloth was joined to reach the required width; sizes such as bepota, dyodha, swaiya and paniya were made by joining lengths.

concepts.summary: An emulsified scouring mix of castor oil, soda ash and camel dung used in saaj; soda ash historically came from desert plant ash.
Dried powdered myrobalan fruit, high in tannin, used as the pre-mordant that gives the cloth a cream-yellow tone.
A paste of lime (chuna) and acacia gum (baval no gund) printed for white outlines; lime also blocks alum and iron.
concepts.body_md: Gum was formerly supplied by Maldhari communities; it is soaked and sieved repeatedly so the paste is smooth.

concepts.summary: Scrap iron fermented with jaggery/molasses and gram flour for 10-15 days; the iron liquor is thickened with gum and printed for black.
The mordant for red, printed in pa and gach pastes.
Boiled powder of roasted, ground tamarind seeds used as the sticky printing base for alum (pa) and to thicken black.
A paste of gum, red clay (lal mitti), water and millet flour; one half receives alum (gach), the other is plain resist (dhori gach).
Sawdust, finely powdered cow dung or rice husk sprinkled on wet resist/mordant prints to prevent smudging.
The blue dye, used as natural indigo cakes fermented in a lime-alkaline vat or as synthetic indigo with hydrosulphite.
concepts.body_md: Indigo was historically brought from Shikarpur in Sindh and a little was grown at Dhamadka.

concepts.summary: Root dye that bonds to the alum mordant to develop red; being revived after near-disappearance.
Coal-tar-derived red (since 1868) that replaced madder; still requires alum.
Galls/flowers of tamarisk added to the red dye bath; also added if colour starts spreading into whites.
Pomegranate rind, turmeric, flame-of-the-forest and marigold for yellow; indigo over yellow for green.
Used both in the neerani scour and in the tapano bleaching soak after madder dyeing.
Sets of 4-6 blocks per design; shisham for the first printing, teak for later stages; registration marks at corners for double-sided printing.
concepts.body_md: Blocks were once carved by printers in spare time; today many are bought from block-makers in Pethapur, while some artisans carve teak blocks themselves.

concepts.summary: A wooden two-handled tray layered with chhapri (grass mat), kantan (jute), foam and fine cotton that holds the printing paste.
A babool-wood paddle used to beat cloth during washing.
A sunken vat maintained continuously, sometimes for decades, by replenishing ingredients.
Red dyeing is carried out in a large copper pot over a low fire, with cloth stirred continuously using two sticks.
Washing historically took place at the river in Dhamadka and now takes place in washing tanks.
Repeated kneading in neerani, overnight steeping in a weighted bundle and sun-drying, 8-10 cycles, until the cloth lathers and turns white and soft.
concepts.body_md: Stage 1 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: The lathered cloth is worked in clean water and beaten with the dhoki until all foam is removed.
concepts.body_md: Stage 2 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Cloth is soaked in harde solution and sun-dried without rinsing; the tannin aids adhesion of later printed mordants.
concepts.body_md: Stage 3 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: White outlines are printed with lime-gum resist; for double-sided ajrakh the same outline is printed on the reverse with precise registration.
concepts.body_md: Stage 4 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Kut paste is printed as infill (datla) between khariyanu outlines; it develops a fast deep black with the tannin on the cloth.
concepts.body_md: Stage 5 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Alum in tamarind-seed paste is printed with blocks carved for the red (mavi) areas, kept clear of lime-printed areas.
concepts.body_md: Stage 6 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Mud-millet-gum paste with alum is printed on larger red areas; it resists indigo and later acts as mordant for red.
concepts.body_md: Stage 7 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Plain mud resist without alum covers remaining white, black and pa-red areas; sawdust or cow dung is sprinkled on the wet paste.
concepts.body_md: Stage 8 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Folded cloth (fara) is dipped in the indigo vat; it turns green then blue on airing; repeated dips (up to 3-4) deepen the blue, with reprinting between dips for two shades.
concepts.body_md: Stage 9 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Gentle then vigorous washing removes clay resists, loose indigo and tamarind paste, leaving indigo, kut black, alum mordants and resisted whites.
concepts.body_md: Stage 10 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Cloth is heated with madder roots or alizarin in a copper pot for up to four hours; red develops on the alum-printed areas, and dried tamarisk flowers are added if colour bleeds.
concepts.body_md:
Stage 11 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

**Fact-check note (2026-10-14):** The "rang" sentence and tamarisk-in-bath detail come from a repeated paragraph that the GI journal places after pa, not from its "Red Dyeing" section; whether they describe the same stage is unclear (see open_question.stage-order-red-indigo).

concepts.summary: After madder dyeing, cloth is soaked in camel dung solution and spread on sandy river banks in the sun, kept moist, for at least three days to clear pink staining.
concepts.body_md: Stage 12 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Final washing and beating, early in the morning in cool water, removes loose colour and brightens the whites.
concepts.body_md: Stage 13 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: Ancillary pressing and packaging before sale.
concepts.body_md: Stage 14 of the sequence as described in the GI method of production (S1).

concepts.summary: The number of neerani cycles depends on the impurities in the cloth; completion is read from a rich lather and bright, soft cloth.
Resist paste is sieved repeatedly to be lump-free and made thicker for finer outlines.
Printers must prevent lime-gum outlines and alum pastes from overlapping, or the red will fail.
Choosing morning, afternoon or late-day printing and early-morning washing according to drying and water temperature.
The dyer decides how many immersions and whether to reprint resists between dips to obtain one or two blues.
The dyer watches for colour bleeding into whites and adds dried tamarisk flowers in response; fire is kept low.
Experienced dyers judge vat condition and shade by tasting, deciding whether lime, soda ash or dates are needed.
Matching the reverse print precisely, using corner registration marks and keeping the fabric partly wet.
Printers choose natural or chemical dyes according to market demand, water conditions and availability.
Blue, red, black and white are required; the GI text reads them as universe, earth, darkness and clouds.
Designs are geometric and symmetric, without figures, recognised by star patterns in geometric borders; Iranian/Islamic influence is suggested.
Traditional ajrakh is printed identically on both faces (bipuri/minakari), regarded as the craft's highest achievement.
Fixed borders on three sides and decorated ends frame a repeating field; named border and field motifs exist.
concepts.body_md: **Fact-check note (2026-10-14):** This passage in the GI journal follows the 1971 Gazetteer quote but also refers to the mid-1990s, so it cannot be attributed to the 1971 Gazetteer as earlier drafts did.

concepts.summary: Specific designs and palettes were reserved for particular client communities and not interchanged; pattern, colour and quality marked hierarchy.
Each design is built from a coordinated set of 4-6 blocks, one per printing layer.
A cloth with deep indigo, madder red, iron black and resisted whites, described as fast.
Lungis, turbans, shoulder cloths, cummerbunds, chaddars, odhanis and ghaghras, bindles, cradle linings and gifts.
Double-sided ajrakh was the most expensive grade; ajrakh also serves as honorary gift.
Saris, dress material, stoles, bed linen; production for designers and international retailers.
Castor oil and alkaline soda ash in neerani emulsify (saponify) to remove waxes, oils and pectin that block absorbency.
concepts.body_md: **Fact-check note (2026-10-14):** Only the GI applicant text supports this; it uses the word "saponification" but no chemistry or scientific source explains how castor oil, soda ash and camel dung act on cotton impurities.

concepts.summary: Alkaline lime in the khariyanu resist discharges alum and resists iron, so lime-printed lines stay white and red fails where they overlap.
Natural madder's more complex colorants stain unmordanted whites pink; sun, moisture and dung compounds in tapano bleach the stain.
Washing in warm afternoon water risks dissolving alum, so the final wash is done in cool morning water.
Process and designs are shared across Sindh, Kutch and Barmer; Kutch ajrakh is described as finer with a wider range of designs than Barmer.
Sources give c. 400-450 years ago, Rao Bharmalji I's reign (1586-1631), the 16th century, c. 1650 (Jinda Jeeva lineage), and a 7th-century flight from Sindh.
Competing derivations: Arabic azraq 'blue'; Sindhi 'aaj rakh' ('keep it today'); 'beautifying'; Persian ajar 'brick' + -ak.

The 1971 Gazetteer describes red dyeing before mud resist and indigo, while the GI method has indigo before the final red dyeing and an ambiguous intermediate 'rang' paragraph; stage counts vary (about 14, 15-16, 16).
The GI text claims indigo/natural-dyed ajrakh 'opens pores' when hot and closes them when cold; no supporting measurement was found.
Sources attribute iron to post-earthquake groundwater change, to river drying and falling water tables, or to the river itself; a quoted 'seven percent iron' figure is unverified.
GI-registered hand block printing of Bagh, Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh, known for geometric repeats in red and black on white using natural colours.
concepts.body_md: Bagh prints are block-printed by hand with wooden blocks and natural (vegetable and mineral) colours, mainly red and black on a white ground. The craft is practised chiefly by the Khatri chhipa community and is known locally as *thappa chhapai* (block printing); it has also been called alizarin printing. The GI specification lists bedcovers, saris, cushion and table covers, dupattas and stoles, durries and dress material among its products.

concepts.summary: Bagh is a small town in Kukshi tehsil, Dhar district, on the Bagh/Baghini river, a tributary of the Narmada; it is also known for the Bagh caves.
concepts.body_md: The GI specification places Bagh at about 22.37 N, 74.77 E, average elevation about 240 m, with Bagh and the Kukshi area as the main production centres. The river is called the Bagh river or Baghini (Baghni) in different sources. Bagh is also known for the Buddhist Bagh caves with mural paintings.

concepts.summary: The Khatri chhipas are believed to have come to Bagh about 400 years ago from Larkana in Sindh, a region famous for Ajrak printing.
concepts.body_md: The GI text reports the belief that Khatri printers came about four centuries ago from Larkana in Sindh, bringing a strong hand block printing tradition, and settled near water sources along the Bagh river. Why they left Sindh is described as not known for sure. One artisan-family narrative also claims a much older family link to the craft (7th century AD), which is not independently documented.

concepts.summary: According to national awardee Ismail Khatri, his ancestors moved from Sindh to Pali, then Gautampur (Malwa), then Manawar (Nimar), with the family settling in Bagh in 1962.
concepts.body_md: Ismail Khatri, described in the GI text as an eminent printer and national awardee, recounted that his ancestors left Sindh, settled in Pali near Jodhpur, moved to Gautampur in Malwa after a famine, and then to Manawar in Nimar. Craft Revival Trust and Gaatha record that the family settled in Bagh in 1962; Craft Revival Trust attributes this to persuasion by local mahajans. The GI text says the quality of the river water helped the settlement.

concepts.summary: The GI text also records a belief that the craft is about a thousand years old and claims that it migrated from Jawad (Mandsaur district) or Rajasthan.
concepts.body_md: Besides the Sindh account, the GI specification notes that some claim the craft migrated from Jawad (Mandsaur district) or Rajasthan, and that it is believed to be roughly a thousand years old, while stating that the exact date of origin is difficult to establish. Craft Revival Trust lists Javad among other former printing centres of Madhya Pradesh (with Ashta, Sehore, Narsinghpur, Khairola) that are now largely extinct.

concepts.summary: Printers formerly made distinct prints and garments for different castes and communities in the region, including Bhil and Bhilala Adivasis; this differentiation has largely gone.
concepts.body_md: The GI text lists communities such as Brahmin, Khatri, Harijan, Bhil, Bhilala, Jat, Bharur and Mahajan as formerly having distinct prints; today only Adivasis keep particular prints, and only for some occasions. Jain describes the prints as originally adornment for tribal inhabitants of surrounding villages. Craft Revival Trust names jaal, choukari, janjuri, juardana and beel among motifs, the latter three as traditional Adivasi sari designs.

concepts.summary: Bagh Prints of Madhya Pradesh was registered as a GI in 2008 (application no. 98); a logo GI (application no. 505) was filed in 2015 and certified in 2016.
concepts.body_md: The applicant for both registrations is the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts), Ministry of Textiles. The logo application (No. 505, Class 24) was advertised in GI Journal No. 75 (26 Nov 2015) and certified (No. 239) on 31 Mar 2016; the registry shows validity to 7 Jan 2025 and renewal status was not confirmed. The GI names the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts), the MP Department of Handicrafts, master artisans and the Textiles Committee as quality-control actors.

concepts.summary: Ismail Sulemanji Khatri (national awardee) and his son Mohammed Yusuf Khatri (Shilp Guru 2017) are publicly recognised for sustaining and reviving Bagh print.
concepts.body_md: The GI text cites Ismail Khatri as an eminent printer and national awardee. Outlook Traveller reports his 1984 national award for a work with 1,230 geometric patterns and says the family has trained over a thousand villagers. The Hitavada reports that Mohammad Yusuf Khatri received the Shilp Guru Award for 2017 for conserving Bagh print. Gaatha credits Ismail Khatri with reviving block printing among the local Adivasi community.

concepts.summary: Mainly cotton (mulmul, cambric, yardage), with silk, tussar, crepe, chiffon, georgette and silk-cotton used as well.
concepts.body_md: The GI specification gives cotton fabric specifications (e.g. mulmul for saris and dupattas, cambric for dress material, yardage for bedcovers) and lists Maheshwari material, kosa silk, bamboo chiks and durries as order-based, with chiffon, crepe, georgette, tissue and mulberry silk occasionally. Silk takes about twice as long as cotton to complete.

concepts.summary: Rock/raw salt used in the mengni (softening) bath.
concepts.body_md: Sanchara is dissolved in water and combined with goat-dung paste and castor oil to form the dhaul solution of mengni karna.

concepts.summary: Ground goat droppings made into paste for the pre-treatment bath.
concepts.body_md: Mengni is soaked, ground with a brick on stone into paste, and mixed with salt and castor oil.

concepts.summary: Unrefined castor oil, curdled with salt into the mengni bath.
concepts.body_md: The GI text specifies unrefined castor oil; Jain instead names linseed oil for the softening step, a discrepancy noted here.

concepts.summary: Myrobalan powder used to give the cloth a yellowish ground and strengthen later red and black.
concepts.body_md: Harara is preferred over bahera because bahera gives a blackish tinge. Down To Earth and Outlook identify harra/harada as Terminalia chebula.

concepts.summary: Colourless mordant printed to produce red after boiling with alizarin and dhavda.
concepts.body_md: Alum is made into a printing paste with tamarind seed powder. Because it is colourless, a simple temporary (chemical) colour is added so the printer can see the print. Varying alum gives different shades of red.

concepts.summary: Iron salt or rusted iron fermented with jaggery, thickened with tamarind seed, printed for black.
concepts.body_md: The GI text gives two recipes: ferrous sulphate mixed with tamarind seed powder and glue cooked in water; and iron sulphate or iron filings left with jaggery and water in an earthen pot for 15–20 days. Hirakayisha was earlier made from iron rust and is now bought.

concepts.summary: Tamarind seed powder used to turn alum and iron solutions into a printable paste.
concepts.body_md: Mordants must first be made into a paint-like solution with tamarind seed; hot water adjusts the density. Colour is generally made each morning for the day.

concepts.summary: Red dye in the bhatti bath that develops alum-printed areas to red and iron areas to black; it replaced the earlier aal root.
concepts.body_md: The GI text says the root of the aal tree was earlier used and alizarine has since taken its place, and that alizarine makes red and black fast. Outlook identifies aal as Morinda tinctoria; Jain notes alizarin originally came from madder (Rubia tinctorum). Whether today's alizarin is synthetic is not stated by these sources.

concepts.summary: Flowers boiled with alizarin in the bhatti; described as giving shine and fixing, collected from local forests.
concepts.body_md: Dhavda flowers are added to the bhatti with alizarin. Sources differ on its role (shine/fixing; yellow; bleaching the harada ground). Both Down To Earth and Outlook identify the bhatti flower as Woodfordia fruticosa; Outlook separately names Anogeissus latifolia as the dhawda plant whose leaves give khaki, so "dhavda/dhavdi" may name two different plants.

concepts.summary: Khaki, mustard, indigo blue and yellow are produced from pomegranate rind, dhavdi leaves, indigo and turmeric.
concepts.body_md: The GI text names four basic natural colours (red, black, khaki, indigo). Mustard is obtained by boiling pomegranate skins 10–12 hours; khaki from dhavdi leaves boiled 10–12 hours; indigo traditionally fermented with lime and sajji in a buried pot for 3 days (now often indigo with caustic and hydro).

concepts.summary: A small amount of bleach is sometimes used to replace repeated stream washing.
concepts.body_md: The GI text reports bleach being added to a drum of water as a time-saving substitute for three to four stream washes.

concepts.summary: Deeply carved teak or sheesham blocks, many made in Pethapur, Gujarat; some in use are about 200 years old.
concepts.body_md: Blocks are intricately carved by block-makers in Pethapur, also sourced from Gandhinagar and Jaipur. Gaatha describes teak blocks drilled with a bow drill (kamthi with saarardi bit), chiselled, and soaked in oil to resist warping and insects; sizes range from about 1 to 16 inches. Craft Revival Trust records the term bilal and that blocks are considered shoji (money and life).

concepts.summary: A tray holding the paste under a bamboo mesh (kartali) and woollen felt; a fine voile layer is added for fine blocks.
concepts.body_md: The GI text describes a wooden tray with cement base (earlier mud), a bamboo mesh (kartali), a loosely woven woollen blanket on top, and a fine voile cotton layer for fine blocks; an earthen pot (mandan) on a grass pot stand balances it.

concepts.summary: A red sandstone printing table; also described as a plank with layers of jute, chaff and cloth.
concepts.body_md: Craft Revival Trust names the red sandstone table farsi; Down To Earth describes a padded plank or table base.

concepts.summary: Large copper vats fixed on brick-and-cement wood-fired furnaces, used to boil printed cloth with alizarin and dhavda.
concepts.body_md: Vats hold about 25 single bedcovers at once; about eight people work a bhatti for six hours using 2–3 quintals of firewood.

concepts.summary: Long wooden sticks used to keep cloth moving in the bhatti.
concepts.body_md: Cloth must be shifted and turned constantly in the hot vat.

concepts.summary: Cloth is soaked and beaten on river stones to remove starch, then dried.
concepts.body_md: The cloth is taken to the river, soaked about two hours, beaten on stones several times, then soaked about an hour more and beaten on a stone slab to remove starch, washed and dried. Jain describes equivalent desizing to stabilise dimensions so motifs are not distorted in later washes.

concepts.summary: Cloth is soaked overnight in a dhaul of rock salt, goat dung and castor oil, foot-pressed, rinsed in the river and dried, repeated three times.
concepts.body_md: Men press the cloth with their feet in the vat for about half an hour until it softens; the cloth then becomes quite soft and is cut into manageable pieces.

concepts.summary: On the following day the cloth is dipped in harara solution in lots and dried, turning yellowish.
concepts.body_md: Lots are dyed about 10 minutes each with harara solution replenished between lots. Gaatha says the yellowed cloth is dried in shade because sun-drying turns it green, whereas Outlook says it is yellowed under controlled sunshine and that over-drying or drying in shade turns it green. Outlook calls this stage peela.

concepts.summary: Alum (red) and iron (black) solutions are prepared and thickened with tamarind seed powder to a printable consistency.
concepts.body_md: Iron black is fermented with jaggery for 15–20 days; Craft Revival Trust records boiling alum or iron sulphate and ageing 8–10 days before thickening with chiyan.

concepts.summary: The block is charged from the felt tray and stamped by hand, outline first; an expert prints about 5 m in 2–3 hours.
concepts.body_md: The printer squats at the table and stamps with a thud of the side of the palm. Gaatha describes stamping a black boundary first and working in rectangles from the outside inwards, masking with old cloth or paper to avoid overlaps.

concepts.summary: Printed cloth is dried, rolled into bundles and kept 8–15 days so the colour sets.
concepts.body_md: Jain gives about seven days; the GI text gives a minimum of eight days to two weeks.

concepts.summary: Two people hold the printed cloth in flowing river water for at least 20 minutes and beat it on stones to remove unfixed colour.
concepts.body_md: If not done correctly, permanent stains and smudges appear. Jain notes washing removes the harda so the fabric becomes white again before alizarin dyeing.

concepts.summary: Washed cloth is boiled in copper vats with dhavda flowers and alizarin, turned constantly, until the red and black develop.
concepts.body_md: The GI text gives about 1.5–2 kg dhavda and 1–1.25 kg alizarin per vat and says heat is increased throughout; Jain says the bath is boiled, then the temperature lowered before immersion. Reported boiling times are about three hours (Down To Earth) and five to six hours (Gaatha); the GI says about eight people work a bhatti for six hours. The GI says each sari goes through the bhatti at least twice over about three weeks.

concepts.summary: Cloth is washed three to four times in the stream and repeatedly sprinkled with water while drying, clearing the ground and setting colours.
concepts.body_md: Outlook describes rinsing three times in running water and sun-bleaching on river stones. A bleach bath may substitute for some washes.

concepts.summary: If colour is not bright enough or two shades are wanted, cloth is re-treated with harara plus alum or iron, then bichalna and bhatti are repeated.
concepts.body_md: Optional loop after tarai; also used for 'double dye' effects.

concepts.summary: Workers decide from experience when to remove cloth from the vat; wrong temperature gives too dark or too weak colour.
concepts.body_md: This is the central tacit judgement of the tradition: the colour develops in the vat and must be read by eye.

concepts.summary: Printers vary the amount of hirakayisha or alum to obtain different shades of black/grey and red.
concepts.body_md: For grey, the cloth is not boiled but passed through lime solution, and harara is not used.

concepts.summary: Because alum is colourless, a simple chemical colour is added so the printer can gauge placement; the real colour appears only after dyeing.
concepts.body_md: Printers must anticipate the final colour from an invisible or temporary print.

concepts.summary: Printers choose harara rather than bahera for the ground because bahera gives a blackish tinge.
concepts.body_md: A material-selection judgement affecting ground colour.

concepts.summary: Permanent smudges from faulty washing can only be hidden by pota, painting the whole surface black or red.
concepts.body_md: The fabric is stretched and painted with a rag tied to a stick.

concepts.summary: Layouts use black and red alternately on a white ground, giving a bold yet harmonious look.
concepts.body_md: Khaki, mustard and indigo are later or secondary colours.

concepts.summary: Geometric patterns are interplaced so the repeat gives a harmonious overall effect; fine blocks distinguish Bagh from bolder MP prints.
concepts.body_md: Down To Earth quotes a printer: only symmetry is to be kept in mind.

concepts.summary: Old blocks carry names such as Nandana, Laheriya, Zanjiri, Mungphali and Chaukada; motifs draw on nature, Bagh cave paintings and Taj Mahal jaali.
concepts.body_md: The GI lists 24 block names (e.g. Nandana, Laheriya, Attha, Makhi, Zanjiri, Jodhpuri, Jawareya, Molya border, Mungphali, Chaukada, Nareyal, Teekoni, Thuddi). Outlook records chameli (jasmine), maithir (mushroom), leheriya (waves), keri (mango) and jurvaria (dots).

concepts.summary: New designs are added about every six months for the market, taking care that each is a variation of an old design.
concepts.body_md: Continuity with the block repertoire is treated as part of the tradition's identity.

concepts.summary: Khatris developed 'double dye' prints such as lal par lal (red on red), lal aur kala and lal aur khaki.
concepts.body_md: Colours are processed one after another or together.

concepts.summary: Alum-printed areas develop from fuchsia pink to a fast red in the alizarin–dhavda bath.
concepts.body_md: Described as the signature colour of the tradition.

concepts.summary: Iron-printed areas become a bright fast black after alizarin dyeing.
Washing and the bhatti remove the yellow harara tint so unprinted areas return to white.
concepts.body_md: Sources attribute this to washing (Jain), to dhavdi bleaching (Gaatha), and to tarai sun-bleaching (Outlook).

concepts.summary: Mordants printed with the blocks react in the alizarin bath to form the final colours: alum gives red, iron gives black, on the same cloth in one bath.
concepts.body_md: Jain describes Bagh dyeing as an indirect method in which mordants applied during printing react with the dyeing compound (alizarin). The GI text says alum absorbs colour on boiling. General chemistry of alum–alizarin complexes and lake formation is covered in the shared mechanisms.

concepts.summary: Iron-printed areas turn black in the alizarin bath; harara (a tannin source) is said to strengthen the black.
concepts.body_md: Sources state that alizarin reacts with iron to give black, and that the harara ground strengthens black and red. Whether the black in Bagh is primarily an iron–alizarin complex or an iron–tannin black (from harara) is not resolved in the sources read.

concepts.summary: The harara (myrobalan) ground is reported as essential for the brightness of the alizarin red and black.
concepts.body_md: This corresponds to tannin pre-mordanting in general dye chemistry (see shared mechanism); the Bagh sources describe the effect but not the chemistry.

concepts.summary: Flowing river water is considered vital for khara, mengni rinsing, bichalna and tarai; proximity to the river is given as the reason for settling at Bagh.
concepts.body_md: The process is described as multi-layered and water-intensive. Gaatha notes that only final washes use the Baghini while other stages use stored tank water.

concepts.summary: The Bagh river dries several times a year, forcing washing at the Narmada; work also slows in the monsoon.
concepts.body_md: The GI text gives the Narmada as about 30 km away in one place and 'five hours away in Chikalda' in another; Craft Revival Trust also records ~40 km. An artisan reports reds and greys fix poorly when washed at the Narmada.

concepts.summary: Several sources claim the Bagh/Baghini water chemistry gives luminous colours, but attribute it to different minerals and present no measurements.
concepts.body_md: The GI text asserts that the river water's chemical composition enhances the red and black. Gaatha attributes it to copper and, elsewhere, iron; an artisan quoted by Craft Revival Trust suggests lime and iron in the soil as a possible scientific reason; the tourism page calls it a belief about minerals. No source read gives water analysis data.

concepts.summary: Indigo-dyed fabric is dried in shade; sources conflict on harara-yellowed cloth (shade per Gaatha, controlled sun per Outlook); tarai uses sun.
concepts.body_md: **Fact-check note (2026-10-14):** Outlook (S6) contradicts Gaatha (S4) on the harara stage: it says the cloth is yellowed under controlled sunshine and that over-drying or drying in shade gives an undesirable green.

concepts.summary: Some artisans use synthetic dyes or bleach to save time and meet demand, while natural dyeing remains the craft's selling point.
Sources disagree on the mineral (copper, iron, lime) and provide no measurements; the claim is untested.
concepts.body_md: A water-quality and colorimetric comparison (Bagh river vs Narmada vs tank water) would be needed to test the claims.

concepts.summary: Two sources identify the bhatti flower (dhavdi/dhawadi) as Woodfordia fruticosa, while one also names Anogeissus latifolia as the "dhawda" whose leaves give khaki; whether one or two plants are meant, and the flower's role (shine/fixing, yellow dye, or bleaching agent), are unresolved.
concepts.body_md: **Fact-check note (2026-10-14):** An earlier draft said the sources conflict (Woodfordia vs Anogeissus) on the bhatti flower; Outlook actually gives Woodfordia fruticosa for the bhatti flower too.

concepts.summary: The GI says alizarine replaced the earlier aal root; other sources describe alizarin as from aal (Morinda) or madder. Current source is not documented.
Accounts range from ~1000 years (local craft), ~400 years (Sindh migration), a 7th-century family claim, to Khatri settlement in Bagh in 1962.
concepts.body_md: These may refer to different things (craft in the region vs a specific family's settlement); documentary evidence is thin, as the GI text itself notes.

concepts.summary: Hand block printing with mostly natural dyes on off-white cotton, practised by the Chhipa community of Bagru near Jaipur; a registered GI since 2011.
concepts.body_md: Bagru prints are stamped with carved wooden blocks, using mostly vegetable dyes, on cotton (sometimes cotton-silk). The GI dossier stresses a few colours on an off-white base, small repetitive motifs, and a production chain split between Chhipa printers/dyers and Kharadi block-makers. Two families of technique are documented in Bagru: direct mordant printing (Syahi-Begar: black and red) and resist printing with mud paste (Dabu) followed by indigo and yellow dyeing.

concepts.summary: Hereditary printers and dyers who live in Bagru's Chhipa Mohalla; they trace descent to Saint Namdev.
concepts.body_md: Chhipas (people who stamp/print) are the hand printers of Bagru, concentrated in the Chhipa Mohalla, which is also the address of the GI applicant society. Gaatha reports that Bagru Chhipas claim descent from Saint Namdev and are classed as OBC; the Titanwala Museum listing calls them Namdev followers. A 2025 survey found Bagru respondents mostly from the Chhipa or Khatri community.

concepts.summary: A separate artisan group (Kharadiya/Kharaodi) carves the wooden printing blocks used by Bagru printers.
concepts.body_md: The GI dossier names turners locally called Kharadiyas as makers of the blocks, using dried woods such as shisham, mango and teak, and kalam chisels for engraving. The Titanwala Museum presents block-making as the work of the Kharaodi community.

concepts.summary: Colonial gazetteer and later scholarship, as compiled in the GI dossier, describe Bagru as famous for dyed and stamped chintzes.
concepts.body_md: The GI dossier quotes the Imperial Gazetteer of India (Rajputana, 1908) that Bagru, about 18 miles south-west of Jaipur, was famous for dyed and stamped chintzes, and cites historians G.N. Sharma and M.L. Gupta for a long-standing industry. It quotes Mohanty & Mohanty (Calico Museum, 1983) that Bagru traditions of printing with natural colours were known for centuries and that, with the attraction of foreign buyers, the village was busy supplying the export trade. These are secondary citations inside an applicant document; the originals were not consulted here.

concepts.summary: Bagru prints historically served local rural communities whose dress codes set colours and motifs.
concepts.body_md: The GI dossier (citing Kapur & Jain and K. Mathur) describes Bagru work as rooted in the local folk milieu, with a limited design and colour range tied to caste- and custom-bound end uses. Printing for Banjara nomads (motifs such as chaupar, camels, horses and doves on dhotis and turbans) is said to have spread to Jats, Gujars, Meenas, Malis and Rajputs. Colours and designs are claimed to identify the user community.

concepts.summary: The GI dossier limits production to Bagru town (main centre) and three villages north of Jaipur.
concepts.body_md: Bagru lies roughly 30 km from Jaipur on the Jaipur-Ajmer road, in Sanganer tehsil. The GI area also includes Kaladera, Jahota and Jairampura (north of Jaipur, Chomu/Amber tehsils).

concepts.summary: Cheaper screen- and digital-printed imitations sold as Bagru, and a shift to chemical dyes, are documented pressures.
concepts.body_md: The GI application itself was motivated by screen-printed fakes sold across India as Bagru prints. A 2025 survey reports chemical dyes now widely used, natural dyes for specific orders, competition from screen/digital printing passed off as block printing, and an industrial park drawing customers away from the old village.

concepts.summary: Mill-made or handloom cotton of different weights is the main substrate; some cotton-silk and other fibres are also used.
concepts.body_md: The GI table lists coarse mill-made latha, handloom cloth, grey superfine mulmul and cambric, matched to product type (e.g. coarse cloth for jajam floor spreads, fine mulmul for chintz).

concepts.summary: Tannin-rich myrobalan powder used as a pre-treatment; gives the cloth its yellowish/cream tint and enables iron-black.
concepts.body_md: Powdered harda is mixed with water and the scoured cloth is soaked in it. Sources call it the most important element of Bagru dyeing; its tannin reacts with the iron syahi to give black.

concepts.summary: A fermented solution of scrap iron (rusted horseshoes/nails) with jaggery, thickened with gum or tamarind starch.
concepts.body_md: Syahi is made by fermenting old iron (horseshoe nails) in water with jaggery/molasses; gum or tamarind-seed starch is added to make a printable paste. On harda-treated cloth it turns black.

concepts.summary: An alum-based paste printed where red is wanted; it becomes red only after the alizarin/madder dyebath.
concepts.body_md: The GI dossier defines begar as the alum mordant that develops a rich red with alizarin. Recipes reported by other sources differ (alum + geru + gum; alum + madder + babul gum; gum + rust + alum) — see open question.

concepts.summary: Madder (Rubia spp.) or, now often, synthetic alizarin is the red dye that reacts with both printed mordants.
concepts.body_md: The alizarin bath is prepared from madder (Rubia tinctorum, Rubia manjista) containing alizarin and purpurin; synthetic alizarin is now common because of shortage of the natural dye.

concepts.summary: Local flowers boiled with alizarin in the dyebath, reported to prevent patches and staining.
concepts.body_md: The GI dossier records that 'dhawai ka phool' is mixed with alizarin in specific ratios; a retailer account also describes boiling red-printed cloth with dhaura flowers and a little oil.

concepts.summary: A resist paste of local black clay (kali mitti), lime, wheat flour/bidhan and gum, with family-specific recipes.
concepts.body_md:
Bagru dabu is made from locally available black clay, slaked lime, wheat flour (including insect-spoiled wheat) and gum, mixed in ratios that depend on the type of dabu needed. It is mashed, left overnight and strained. Each family keeps its own recipe.

Fact-check note (2026-10-14): Sources disagree on the term 'bidhan': the GI dossier glosses lime as 'Bidhan', Raj (2012) uses 'Bedhan' for a natural gum (or worm-spoiled wheat flour), and The Kind Craft glosses wheat powder as 'bidhan'.

concepts.summary: Sprinkled on freshly printed dabu to absorb water, add a resist layer and stop the cloth sticking to itself.
concepts.body_md: Sawdust is dusted onto the wet dabu prints before they dry.

concepts.summary: Blue dye from Indigofera tinctoria (now often synthetic) used in deep vats for dabu work.
concepts.body_md: Indigo vats are kept 'alive' by adding indigo, lime and jaggery; synthetic indigo granules are also used.

concepts.summary: A yellow dye extract (haldi + naspal) applied over indigo to obtain Bagru green.
concepts.body_md: Turmeric (haldi) and pomegranate rind (naspal/anar chhilka) are fugitive yellows that need an alum after-mordant.

concepts.summary: Used both as the begar mordant and as a dilute after-mordant bath that fixes yellow and loosens dabu.
concepts.body_md: Alum dissolved in water and strained is used in a short bath after yellow dyeing.

concepts.summary: Traditional desizing/scouring used cow dung (later soap), sometimes with soda ash and sesame oil.
concepts.body_md: The GI lists a 'telkhar' emulsion for oiling and alkaline treatment to desize and partially bleach grey cloth.

concepts.summary: Hand-carved hardwood blocks with handles; a design uses a set of background, outline and filler blocks.
concepts.body_md: Blocks are rectangular, square, round, oval or segmental (a quarter-circle block is 'chand'). Woods include shisham, teak, mango and rohida. New blocks are soaked in oil for about 10-15 days; Gaatha gives a working life of 600-800 m of printing. A cloth typically needs 4-5 blocks.

concepts.summary: Steel chisels of different widths used by block-carvers to engrave motifs.
concepts.body_md: Carvers also use drills, hammers, nails and files.

concepts.summary: Long padded tables for standing printers; low tables for seated dabu printing.
concepts.body_md: The GI lists a long 'mej' table printers walk around and a low 'pathiya' used mainly for dabu by older printers and women who sit. Tables are padded with many layers of cloth (jute/canvas) under the fabric.

concepts.summary: A shallow tray with a frame and layered cloth pad that spreads paste evenly onto the block.
concepts.body_md: Each colour needs its own tray; the block is pressed into the saturated pad before every impression. A wheeled trolley (gadi) carries trays around the table.

concepts.summary: Large wood-fired copper vessels used for the alizarin dyebath and alum baths.
concepts.body_md: Alizarin is placed in small cloth bags and dipped into the heated vessel.

concepts.summary: Deep in-ground vats in which dabu-printed cloth is repeatedly dipped.
concepts.body_md:
Reported depths vary (10-12 ft; about 15 ft).

Fact-check note (2026-10-14): Gaatha uses 'maat' for a clay container in which synthetic indigo is reduced, distinct from the in-ground 'naand'.

concepts.summary: Wooden mallets beat harda-treated or washed cloth; dabu is beaten off on stone slabs in flowing water.
concepts.body_md: Fact-check note (2026-10-14): Terminology conflicts: the GI dossier calls the wooden mallet 'mogri', whereas Gaatha describes the 'mogari' as a cylindrical wooden roller on which cloth is beaten with a 'kotan'.

concepts.summary: Grey cloth is soaked in cow-dung (now soap) liquor, then repeatedly wetted and sun-dried for days until white.
concepts.body_md: Removes starch, oil and dust so colours penetrate evenly. Traditionally cloth was soaked overnight in cow dung and water, washed, spread on open ground and re-wetted 5-6 times a day for 3-6 days.

concepts.summary: Cloth is soaked in harda solution, squeezed, dried flat and beaten to remove excess powder.
concepts.body_md: Gives the cream/yellow ground and prepares the cloth to react with iron and alum mordants.

concepts.summary: Blocks print the iron syahi (usually outline) and alum begar (filler) onto the harda-treated cloth.
concepts.body_md: The printer charges the block on the pad and stamps it on the padded table. Syahi is usually printed with the rekh (outline) block; because it shows black immediately, a second printer can register the begar filler block against it. Sometimes the background block is applied first.

concepts.summary: Printed cloth is left at least 3-4 days so the mordant paste penetrates the fibre.
Printed cloth is washed in running water to remove unfixed mordant and gum.
Cloth is boiled with alizarin and dhawai flowers in a copper vessel for about half a day; red develops on begar, black on syahi.
concepts.body_md: One dyebath reacts with two mordants at two locations to give red and black. The dyed cloth is then laid on the ground to dry.

concepts.summary: Dabu paste is block-printed over areas to be protected, dusted with sawdust and sun-dried.
concepts.body_md: Because the paste is thick and sticky, sharp definition is not achieved. Traditionally women did dabu printing, though men now also do it.

concepts.summary: Pleated cloth is lowered into the vat, opened under the liquor, lifted to oxidise, and re-dipped until the desired depth.
concepts.body_md: The first dip gives pale sky blue; repeated dip-and-air cycles darken it (one source says up to 6 dips). Cloth is dried flat without cracking the dabu.

concepts.summary: After re-printing dabu to keep some blue, a turmeric-pomegranate yellow is mopped on while four people hold the cloth taut.
concepts.body_md: A fifth person rubs the yellow on with a loose-woven woollen cloth acting as a sponge, gently so the dabu does not come off.

concepts.summary: A brief dip in dilute alum fixes the yellow; cloth is then stored folded in the dark for 3-4 days.
Cloth is soaked 3-4 hours to soften the resist, then beaten on stone in flowing water; dried in the sun and finished.
concepts.body_md: The GI notes effluent is aerated before discharge and that units planned a common effluent treatment plant.

concepts.summary: Printers choose which block goes first and align repeats visually; printing the black outline first makes filler placement visible.
concepts.body_md: Practitioners decide the number of blocks from the number of colours and shapes. Accounts differ on whether background or outline goes first.

concepts.summary: The amount of alizarin is calculated by the experienced dyer rather than by fixed formula.
Experts judge the vat's state by its colour and add ingredients by experience; no written recipe exists.
Dabu recipes are varied by family and by how many vat immersions the resist must survive.
concepts.body_md: Raj (2012) names three types: kaligar (single process), dolidar (more gum, about two trips), gawarbali (oil and guar seed powder, repeated dyeing).

concepts.summary: Dyers unfold pleats gently under the liquor, and limit alum dip time, to avoid patchy dye or dabu loss.
Bagru prints sit on an off-white to cream (harda-tinted) ground, versus Sanganer's white.
Traditional Bagru prints are in red and black, with the black carrying a reddish tinge.
Motifs are small, repetitive and drawn from flowers/leaves/buds, tendrils, trellis, figurative and geometric groups.
concepts.body_md: Named motifs reported include aath kaliyan, bankadi, hajura, hara dhania, kamal, chopad, kel, pyala and chhota bel (Raj 2012), and leher, chaupad, kangura and jaali (The Kind Craft).

concepts.summary: A design is decomposed into a gadh (background), rekh (outline) and one datta per additional colour.
Practitioners note busy traditional patterns hide dye drips that sparse modern layouts reveal.
Black and red motifs on a cream ground, produced by printing two mordants and dyeing once in alizarin.
Light motifs reserved against indigo; plant motifs on a dark indigo ground are presented as a Bagru peculiarity.
concepts.body_md: Repeated resist-and-dye cycles can produce tonal gradients. A 19th-century Bagru mud-resist garment in the Penn Museum shows a purple ground with small red flowers.

concepts.summary: Green obtained by over-dyeing indigo with a turmeric/pomegranate yellow fixed by alum.
Alizarin forms different coloured complexes with aluminium (red) and iron (black/dark), so one bath gives two colours where the mordants were printed.
concepts.body_md: The GI dossier states the dye reacts with two mordants at two locations to give red and black. The general chemistry (metal–alizarin lake formation) is covered by the shared mechanisms; unmordanted areas are cleared in later washing/sunning per general practice (not specifically sourced for Bagru).

concepts.summary: Tannic acid from harda reacts with ferrous iron in syahi to form black where printed.
The dried clay-lime-gum layer physically blocks dye penetration; sawdust adds a further layer.
Cloth taken from the vat turns blue as reduced indigo oxidises in air; each dip adds depth.
Turmeric/pomegranate yellow is fugitive; an alum bath makes it fast.
Abundant flowing water and the river's sandy bed are said to have drawn Chhipas to Bagru; the river now runs dry.
concepts.body_md: Sources claim the local water has properties suited to dyeing and that the Sanjaria waters gave finished cloth a sheen; these are unverified claims. Nearly every stage needs washing.

concepts.summary: Cloth is repeatedly spread on open ground to dry and whiten between stages.
Semi-arid, hot climate; production follows seasons and monsoon rain halts outdoor work.
concepts.body_md: The GI dossier gives annual rainfall of about 56.6 cm and a temperature range of 0.5–48 °C for the area; Gaatha gives about 650 mm monsoon rain (June–September).

concepts.summary: Declining rainfall and water table threaten production; chemical-dye effluent pollutes groundwater.
Neighbouring centres ~30 km apart: Bagru folk, off-white/cream, limited palette; Sanganer courtly, white ground.
concepts.body_md: The GI dossier quotes Kapur & Jain that Bagru work is rooted in the folk milieu in contrast to Sanganer's courtly sensibility, and notes museum labels have confused the two.

concepts.summary: Estimates range from 300 to 450+ years and no authentic record fixes the start.
concepts.body_md: The GI dossier says Chhipas settled about 300 years ago (and elsewhere calls Bagru a 16th-century town); Gaatha and Raj give 450 years (and 400); The Kind Craft says at least 400; Wikipedia cites 400–470. Raj notes there is no authentic record.

concepts.summary: Sources disagree on begar ingredients and one source reverses the rekh/datta names.
concepts.body_md: Begar is given as alum alone (GI), alum + geru + gum (Raj), alum + madder + babul gum (Kind Craft, Kaisori), or gum + rust + alum (Gaatha). The GI, Gaatha and The Kind Craft call the outline block 'rekh' and the filler 'datta'; Kaisori reverses this and says blocks come from Pethapur.

concepts.summary: The registry shows certificate 150 dated 11-05-2011; Wikipedia claims a 2024 grant.
Sources agree synthetics (alizarin, indigo, other dyes) are widely used but give no quantified share.
The 'excellent properties' of Bagru water and the Sanjaria sheen are asserted but not tested in any source found.
concepts.body_md: No water-chemistry study for Bagru was found.

concepts.summary: Dabu is a Rajasthani hand-block printing technique in which a mud-based paste is block-printed onto cloth as a resist before dyeing, most often in indigo. Akola village (Chittorgarh district) is widely described as its centre of origin.
concepts.body_md: Printers press carved wooden blocks dipped in a mud, lime and gum paste onto cloth; the pasted areas resist the dye bath, and resist-and-dye cycles are repeated to build shades. The name is linked to the Hindi *dabaana*, "to press". Akola is documented as a self-sufficient Dabu cluster run by the Chhipa printing community; the technique is also recorded in Bagru (Rajasthan) and Deesa (Gujarat).

concepts.summary: Akola (Chhipo ka Akola) lies in Bhupalsagar/Bhopalsagar tehsil of Chittorgarh district, about 52 km west of Chittorgarh, on the Beduch river; around 200 people practise the craft there.
concepts.body_md:
Gaatha records a founding tradition that a queen of Mewar (Rani Rathorji) settled the Chhipa printers by the Beduch river a few hundred years ago. Fabric (20x20 count cotton) is sourced from Kishangarh and pigments from Udaipur. Some sources place Akola in Udaipur district instead (see open question).

Fact-check note: the alternative name "Chhipo ka Akola" rests only on a Wikipedia statement tagged [citation needed]; the founding tradition is undated in Gaatha ("hundreds of years ago").

concepts.summary: Dabu in Akola is practised by the Chhipa (Chippa) block-printing community, historically working with Neelgars (indigo dyers), Rangrez (dyers) and Dhobis (washermen).
concepts.body_md: The community name is linked to *chhapna*, to print. Craft Revival Trust notes that dabu printing at Bagru is often done by women at home or in workshops (*karkhanas*). AIACA instead attributes Dabu to the Khatri community (see open question).

concepts.summary: Dabu is named from dabaana (to press); a widely repeated legend credits a dyer whose mud-stained cloth stayed undyed in indigo.
