concepts.body_md: Gaatha relates the legend of a Rangrez whose dhoti picked up riverside mud and showed an unstained patch after indigo dyeing; Deccan Chronicle notes the story is unverified.

concepts.summary: Sources give conflicting ages for Dabu, from an 8th-century AD Central Asian specimen to "about 675 AD", "500 years" and "200-year legacy" in Akola.
concepts.body_md: None of the accessible sources cites a dated, catalogued specimen directly. The earliest firm object evidence found is a mid-to-late 19th-century mud-resist textile from Bagru in the Penn Museum.

concepts.summary: Dabu clusters across Rajasthan dwindled with machine printing and changing dress; revival since the 2000s involves NGOs and enterprises such as Aavaran (founded 2009 in Akola).
concepts.body_md: Gaatha notes Rajasthan once had many Dabu clusters of which very few remain. Deccan Chronicle reports Aavaran set up a self-help group in Akola in 2009, keeping the traditional process but adding contemporary motifs.

concepts.summary: A GI application for "Aakola Dabu Prints" (No. 845, Class 24) was filed on 4 March 2022 and stood at Pre Examination on the access date; it is not a registered GI.
concepts.body_md: A separate GI application for Deesa Dabu Block Print of Gujarat was noted in search results but not fetched. AIACA states Dabu received a GI tag in 2023, which the registry record does not support.

concepts.summary: Akola Dabu was printed for community-specific garments such as the phetiya (long ghagra skirt) worn by Jat, Gujjar and Gadariya women, often with a bandhej lugda head-cloth.
concepts.body_md: A phetiya was a single 8-12 m cloth joined with one line of stitching. Global InCH distinguishes two Akola dabu types, phetia (Jat and Chaudhury women, after childbirth or at weddings) and nangna (Gujjar women). Contemporary products include dupattas, stoles and saris with separate border, pallu and body designs.

concepts.summary: Beyond Akola, mud-resist Dabu is recorded at Bagru (Rajasthan), Deesa, Ahmedabad and Jamnagar (Gujarat), and historically at Tarapur, Bhilwara and Pahuna.
concepts.body_md: This dataset centres on Akola; Bagru is covered as its own tradition elsewhere and is cited here only where sources document Dabu there.

concepts.summary: The resist base is local mud or clay; sources variously describe black clay dug from a dry pond, riverbank mud, or river-bed silt.
concepts.body_md: Mud is soaked in water (overnight, in a separate tank) before mixing. In Akola the earth "lends mud"; Kaisori links it to the dry arid region. One supplier describes fine desert sand.

concepts.summary: Lime is a standard ingredient of the Dabu paste; on its own, lime (kirana) is described as the weakest resist, used for fine outlines.
concepts.body_md: Lime is a standard ingredient of the Dabu paste; on its own, lime (kirana) is described as the weakest resist, used for fine outlines.

concepts.summary: A natural gum binds the paste; sources name babul/acacia seed gum, neem gum, baval gum and a local gum.
concepts.body_md: A natural gum binds the paste; sources name babul/acacia seed gum, neem gum, baval gum and a local gum.

concepts.summary: A wheat by-product appears in many recipes: "waste wheat chaff" or beedan, moth-eaten wheat-flour waste.
concepts.body_md: Sources differ on whether wheat waste is mixed into the paste (Akola, Bagru accounts) or used as the dusting powder (Craft Revival Trust, Bagru).

concepts.summary: The Craft Revival Trust records sugarcane molasses as a paste ingredient in Deesa, Gujarat.
concepts.body_md: The Craft Revival Trust records sugarcane molasses as a paste ingredient in Deesa, Gujarat.

concepts.summary: Secondary sources describe several named resist recipes and strengths: kalidar (black clay, chuna, beedan, gond), dolidar (gond, chuna, Multani mitti), gawarvali (roasted guar bean powder with lime and gum), and a sand (rait) resist.
concepts.body_md: Global InCH ranks three Akola resists: chuna/lime weakest (fine outlines), mitti/mud (repeated indigo immersion), rait/sand strongest (absorbent colours like pomegranate and ferrous dyes). Families reportedly keep their own recipes.

concepts.summary: Sawdust is sprinkled onto freshly printed wet paste to dry it quickly, fix it in place and prevent smudging.
concepts.body_md: Sawdust is sprinkled onto freshly printed wet paste to dry it quickly, fix it in place and prevent smudging.

concepts.summary: Indigo is the principal dye of Dabu, used in a cold bath into which the resist-printed cloth is dipped repeatedly.
concepts.body_md: Indigo is the principal dye of Dabu, used in a cold bath into which the resist-printed cloth is dipped repeatedly.

concepts.summary: The Lal Titri red of Akola was traditionally alizarin; naphthol, developed with "red salt", has replaced it.
concepts.body_md: The Lal Titri red of Akola was traditionally alizarin; naphthol, developed with "red salt", has replaced it.

concepts.summary: Akola prints on cotton (20x20 count) from Kishangarh; Dabu has spread to silk, crepe and georgette.
concepts.body_md: Akola prints on cotton (20x20 count) from Kishangarh; Dabu has spread to silk, crepe and georgette.

concepts.summary: In present-day Akola, a mixture of tar, oil and rogan applied with blocks has largely replaced mud as the resist, with ash sprinkled to dry it; the tar is boiled off and reused.
concepts.body_md: Gaatha says the change was for finer designs, since mud mostly cracked and changed the look. Global InCH similarly describes a boiled gum-and-oil hot resist dusted with ash.

concepts.summary: A low-reliability Bagru account describes a harda (myrobalan) wash whose tannin mordants the iron black, and an alum-water rinse that fixes colour on dabu-printed cloth; none of the Akola sources confirms these steps.
concepts.body_md:
A low-reliability Bagru account describes a harda (myrobalan) wash whose tannin mordants the iron black, and an alum-water rinse that fixes colour on dabu-printed cloth; none of the Akola sources confirms these steps.

Fact-check note: the earlier claim (harda pretreatment plus alum/iron mordants for alizarin reds and iron-harda blacks) rested only on the Wikipedia "Dabu printing" article, which carries an LLM-generated-content warning and cites mismatched references; it was replaced with Bagru-specific statements from S23. The Penn Museum catalogue (S11) confirms only that a 19th-century Bagru mud-resist cloth was mordant dyed.

concepts.summary: Hand-carved wooden blocks, made by carvers in Akola itself, are dipped in the paste and pressed onto cloth.
concepts.body_md: Block woods named include sheesham, rohira and teak (carved by batkare carpenters). Akola once had 14 traditional block designs.

concepts.summary: Printing is done on low wooden tables (Akola: about 150 x 60 cm), either seated at a single table or on a running table.
concepts.body_md: Printing is done on low wooden tables (Akola: about 150 x 60 cm), either seated at a single table or on a running table.

concepts.summary: Cloth is dipped in an indigo vat; Akola also uses wood or plastic dyeing trays.
concepts.body_md: Cloth is dipped in an indigo vat; Akola also uses wood or plastic dyeing trays.

concepts.summary: The paste is strained before use and, per one secondary source, strained through fine muslin and stored in a clay pot called a mardia.
concepts.body_md: The paste is strained before use and, per one secondary source, strained through fine muslin and stored in a clay pot called a mardia.

concepts.summary: Large kadhai-like boilers, set up with government support, are used in Akola to boil off the tar resist.
concepts.body_md: Large kadhai-like boilers, set up with government support, are used in Akola to boil off the tar resist.

concepts.summary: Mud or black clay is collected (from a dry pond or riverbank) and soaked in water overnight.
concepts.body_md: Mud or black clay is collected (from a dry pond or riverbank) and soaked in water overnight.

concepts.summary: Soaked mud is mixed with lime, gum and wheat waste, kneaded (in Deesa by stamping over several days) and strained into a smooth viscous paste.
concepts.body_md: Soaked mud is mixed with lime, gum and wheat waste, kneaded (in Deesa by stamping over several days) and strained into a smooth viscous paste.

concepts.summary: Grey cloth is washed to remove impurities (and starch) that could block dyeing, then sun-dried.
concepts.body_md:
Grey cloth is washed to remove impurities (and starch) that could block dyeing, then sun-dried.

Fact-check note: the dung-scouring detail is documented only for Bagru by a low-reliability source (S23); the earlier Wikipedia-only claim of a 24-hour dung soak was removed. Akola sources describe only a wash to remove impurities.

concepts.summary: Before resist, coloured areas may be block-printed with fast dyes; in Akola, naphthol is printed and developed in red salt.
concepts.body_md: Before resist, coloured areas may be block-printed with fast dyes; in Akola, naphthol is printed and developed in red salt.

concepts.summary: Blocks dipped in the paste are pressed onto the areas that must stay undyed.
concepts.body_md: Blocks dipped in the paste are pressed onto the areas that must stay undyed.

concepts.summary: The wet paste is immediately dusted with sawdust (or beden, or ash for tar) to dry it and prevent smudging.
concepts.body_md: The wet paste is immediately dusted with sawdust (or beden, or ash for tar) to dry it and prevent smudging.

concepts.summary: The printed cloth is spread in hot sun until the paste hardens completely.
concepts.body_md: The printed cloth is spread in hot sun until the paste hardens completely.

concepts.summary: The dried cloth is dip-dyed, typically in a cold indigo bath, re-dipped until the shade is reached.
concepts.body_md: The dried cloth is dip-dyed, typically in a cold indigo bath, re-dipped until the shade is reached.

concepts.summary: Out of the vat the cloth turns from green to blue as indigo oxidises, and is dried again.
concepts.body_md: Out of the vat the cloth turns from green to blue as indigo oxidises, and is dried again.

concepts.summary: Paste and excess dye are washed out (in Akola on the Beduch river banks; tar resist is boiled off), revealing the undyed pattern.
concepts.body_md: Paste and excess dye are washed out (in Akola on the Beduch river banks; tar resist is boiled off), revealing the undyed pattern.

concepts.summary: The resist-and-dye sequence is repeated, through a dye bath per colour, building layered shades ("double" or "triple" dabu).
concepts.body_md: The resist-and-dye sequence is repeated, through a dye bath per colour, building layered shades ("double" or "triple" dabu).

concepts.summary: Printers choose a resist according to line fineness and dye: lime for fine outlines, mud for repeated indigo dips, sand for strongly absorbent dyes.
concepts.body_md: Printers choose a resist according to line fineness and dye: lime for fine outlines, mud for repeated indigo dips, sand for strongly absorbent dyes.

concepts.summary: The paste must be kneaded and strained to a smooth viscous body that transfers cleanly from the block.
concepts.body_md:
The paste must be kneaded and strained to a smooth viscous body that transfers cleanly from the block.

Fact-check note: an earlier claim that the paste is "freshly prepared before every printing" was not found in its cited source (S17) and was removed.

concepts.summary: Printers dust the wet paste at once to stop smudging, and wait until it is fully hardened before dipping.
concepts.body_md: Analogous clay-resist practice also stresses complete drying before submersion.

concepts.summary: The dyer repeats indigo dips until the required shade is reached, and decides how many resist-dye cycles to run for the colour scheme.
concepts.body_md: The dyer repeats indigo dips until the required shade is reached, and decides how many resist-dye cycles to run for the colour scheme.

concepts.summary: Akola printers moved to tar for finer, sharper designs because mud cracked and changed the look; cracking is thus a defect in one framing and a valued effect in another.

concepts.summary: Dabu motifs are taken from nature and the local surroundings, then carved onto blocks; symmetry is noted.

concepts.summary: Of 14 traditional Akola blocks, four main motifs survive: Kahma, Lal Titri, Dholika and Kantedar; Lal Titri, the signature, covered phetiyas with an overall ground print and zigzag border in red and indigo.
concepts.body_md: Of 14 traditional Akola blocks, four main motifs survive: Kahma, Lal Titri, Dholika and Kantedar; Lal Titri, the signature, covered phetiyas with an overall ground print and zigzag border in red and indigo.

concepts.summary: Design is conceived negatively: what is printed with paste stays the ground colour while the rest takes the dye, so motifs appear light on indigo.

concepts.summary: Multi-tone effects come from successive resist-and-dye layers, each protecting the previous shade.
concepts.body_md: Multi-tone effects come from successive resist-and-dye layers, each protecting the previous shade.

concepts.summary: Patterns, colours and cloth formats were tied to the wearer's community and occasion (phetia vs nangna; Jat, Gujjar, Gadariya).
concepts.body_md: Patterns, colours and cloth formats were tied to the wearer's community and occasion (phetia vs nangna; Jat, Gujjar, Gadariya).

concepts.summary: Washing off the resist reveals the undyed (or previously dyed) pattern against the indigo ground.
concepts.body_md: Washing off the resist reveals the undyed (or previously dyed) pattern against the indigo ground.

concepts.summary: Where the dried mud cracks, dye seeps in, giving fine veins; this is valued as a Dabu signature but was a reason Akola adopted tar for fine work.
concepts.body_md: Where the dried mud cracks, dye seeps in, giving fine veins; this is valued as a Dabu signature but was a reason Akola adopted tar for fine work.

concepts.summary: Repeated cycles produce cloth in shades of indigo with red (Lal Titri) and soil-brown tones.
concepts.body_md: Repeated cycles produce cloth in shades of indigo with red (Lal Titri) and soil-brown tones.

concepts.summary: A dried clay paste survives only short, cold immersions; indigo dyeing is cold and quick, so the mud stays in place, whereas hot, prolonged natural-dye baths would wash it off.
concepts.body_md: This explains why Dabu is so closely tied to indigo, and why Akola reds are produced by printing (naphthol) rather than by hot dyeing over mud. Evidence is educational/practitioner, not Dabu-specific laboratory work.

concepts.summary: As the paste dries it shrinks and cracks; dye penetrates the cracks and stains thin lines in the reserved area.
concepts.body_md: Sources describe the effect and the shrinkage (puckering) qualitatively; a Met conservator documents dye penetration through resist cracks under 10x magnification of a historic fragment, but no measured study of Dabu paste cracking was found.

concepts.summary: Sawdust or beden dusted on the wet paste quickens drying and prevents smudging and sticking; for tar, ash plays the same role.
concepts.body_md: Sources state the function; the physical mechanism (absorbing surface moisture, forming a non-stick layer) is not explicitly established in the sources.

concepts.summary: In Akola, printed naphthol is developed by dipping in "red salt", which reacts with it to form a bright red.
concepts.body_md: Gaatha's archive gives a general account of the naphthol (azoic) process; no Akola-specific chemical analysis was found.

concepts.summary: Drying of the resist relies on hot sun; the arid region also supplies the mud.
concepts.body_md: Drying of the resist relies on hot sun; the arid region also supplies the mud.

concepts.summary: Akola depends on the Beduch river, plus hand pumps and tube wells; the craft archive calls for water reuse and reports that chemical residues pollute groundwater.
concepts.body_md: Akola depends on the Beduch river, plus hand pumps and tube wells; the craft archive calls for water reuse and reports that chemical residues pollute groundwater.

concepts.summary: Gaatha reports high water use, chemical residues polluting local groundwater, and hazardous tar fumes and ash dust in Akola.
concepts.body_md: Gaatha reports high water use, chemical residues polluting local groundwater, and hazardous tar fumes and ash dust in Akola.

concepts.summary: Daboo is grouped with Rajasthani block prints such as Bagru and Sanganeri but is described as distinct from them in look and method.

Fact-check note: a mud-versus-wax (batik) contrast rested only on the Wikipedia article with an LLM-content warning and was removed.

concepts.summary: Sources disagree: black clay vs riverbank mud vs river silt vs desert sand; wheat chaff in the paste vs wheat waste as dusting; molasses (Deesa) and guar (gawarvali) only in some accounts; AIACA calls it fermented.
concepts.body_md: No laboratory analysis of Dabu paste was found; the key academic sources (Kaur; Mehta et al. 2013; Hada & Meena 2022) were not accessible.

concepts.summary: Gaatha's archive says Akola now uses tar/oil/rogan (and Global InCH a boiled gum-oil hot resist), while journalism and craft profiles describe ongoing mud resist; the share of each is unknown.
concepts.body_md: Gaatha's archive says Akola now uses tar/oil/rogan (and Global InCH a boiled gum-oil hot resist), while journalism and craft profiles describe ongoing mud resist; the share of each is unknown.

concepts.summary: Origin dates range from the 8th century to 200 years; Akola is placed in Chittorgarh by most sources but Udaipur by Global InCH; AIACA credits the Khatri community while Akola sources name the Chhipas.

concepts.summary: A mordant- and vegetable-dye, hand-block-printed cotton textile tradition of Pedana and neighbouring villages near Machilipatnam, Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh, registered as the GI "Machilipatnam Kalamkari".
concepts.body_md: Machilipatnam Kalamkari is the block-printed branch of Andhra kalamkari. Designs are carved into wooden blocks and printed onto cotton with mordants (iron "kasim", alum "karam") and dyes, then developed by boiling and fixed through repeated washing and sun-drying. Production today is centred on Pedana and organised in workshops (karkhanas). It is registered as a Geographical Indication (application no. 90).

concepts.summary: Production under the GI is limited to Pedana town and neighbouring villages including Machilipatnam, Polavaram and Kappaladoddi (Guduru mandal), Krishna district.
concepts.body_md: Sources consistently place present-day block-printed kalamkari in Pedana rather than in Machilipatnam town itself, with Kappaladoddi and Polavaram as further centres. The district ODOP list of authorised suppliers is mostly in Pedana, with single units in Polavaram, Machilipatnam and Vijayawada.

concepts.summary: Masulipatnam was the Golconda Sultanate's port; its painted and printed cottons were patronised by the Golconda rulers in the 16th–17th centuries and designed to Islamic/Persian taste.
concepts.body_md: Scholarly and museum sources describe Masulipatnam as a major textile-trading port of the Golconda kingdom, with kalamkari made for the Sultanate and for Persia. Asia InCH says the craft began in Golconda and spread along the eastern coast. The district ODOP page adds that the style developed under Mughal rule and was practised under the Golconda Sultanate.

concepts.summary: Masulipatnam cloth was exported to Persia from the 17th century; V&A pieces of the 19th century were printed for the Iranian market and carry Persian inscriptions.
concepts.body_md: A V&A dress fabric of 1879 bears a Persian inscription naming a trader and calling itself "qalamkar", with shipping letters indicating Masulipatam. Another V&A quilted cover was catalogued as printed by Iranian craftsmen in Masulipatam for the Iranian market. Ghosh records that the link with Persia was broken in 1924.

concepts.summary: Mordant-dyed and resist-dyed Coromandel cottons ("chintz") were imported in large quantities into Britain and the Netherlands in the 17th–18th centuries; Masulipatnam was a key centre.
concepts.body_md: Kalamkari textiles were originally known in the West as Coromandel chintz; the English called them chintz, the Dutch sitz and the Portuguese pintado. Designs were adapted for European, Persian and Southeast Asian markets.

concepts.summary: At Masulipatnam, hand-drawn (kalam) work was progressively replaced by carved wooden blocks, a change sources date to the 19th century and link to repetitive designs.
concepts.body_md: Museum and craft sources agree that block printing came to dominate Masulipatnam production, with the kalam retained for finer details or wax resist; later decline and revival phases are recorded (decline by the 2nd quarter of the 20th century; revival from 1952 with the All India Handicrafts Board).

concepts.summary: GI application no. 90 was filed on 16 April 2007 and the certificate (no. 71) issued 10 July 2008; secondary sources give 2012 or 2013, apparently reflecting authorised-user registration/certificate handover.
concepts.body_md: The GI Registry record is the primary source for dates. SpicyIP (2013) reports members of the Pedana printers' welfare association receiving the certificate and cites authorised-user number AU/396/GI/19/12; later secondary sources repeat 2012 or 2013 as the GI year.

concepts.summary: Production is organised in commercial workshops (karkhanas) where block making, washing and printing occur together; craft documentation names Devanga, Padmasali, Kannebhaktulu and Senapathalu communities, with Hindu and Muslim dyers/printers.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark lists the main castes engaged as Devangas, Padmasalis, Kannebhaktulu and Senapathalu, who weave as well as dye and print; dyers and printers were Hindu or Muslim; blocks were made by specialist block makers. Sahapedia notes block makers are mostly from the carpenter community and that the printing technique is said to have been introduced by the rangrez (dyer) community. A Pedana printers' welfare association is the GI applicant.

concepts.summary: The ground is unbleached (kora) cotton long cloth, typically 20s or 60s count.
concepts.body_md: All process sources use cotton as the substrate; Craftmark specifies kora long cloth of 20 or 60 counts. Recent work also experiments with Mangalagiri and other cottons.

concepts.summary: A tannin-rich myrobalan (Terminalia chebula) solution is applied to the bleached cloth before printing; it also serves as a yellow dye.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark describes pounding myrobalan in a stone pot, boiling it with water for at least 2.5 hours, cooling, filtering and keeping it overnight. The cloth is dipped briefly, squeezed and sun-dried, taking on a yellowish tint. Sources disagree on whether the plant part is the dried flower or the fruit.

concepts.summary: Fermented iron liquor — iron strips/scrap with jaggery and salt water — used to print black outlines.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark gives a recipe: iron strips are heated in burning paddy husk overnight, scrubbed of rust, then covered with a jaggery and salt-water solution in a stone pot set about 90% below ground and sealed. A journalist's account gives iron scrap, jaggery and salt water in a mud jar buried for 21 days. It is called kasim (also "kasimkaram" in a peer-reviewed source on related Tamil kalamkari).

concepts.summary: Alum, called karam in Telugu, is the mordant printed where red/pink is wanted and used in a final fixing bath.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark: pounded alum crystals boiled in water (4 L to 3.5 kg) until reduced by half; for printing it is thickened with gum. Iron utensils are avoided because iron darkens the colour. The district page adds that different alum concentrations give more shades. Sahapedia's claim that alum is not used for red at Machilipatnam conflicts with this.

concepts.summary: Red is developed by boiling alum-printed cloth in alizarin; historically red came from madder and chay root (Oldenlandia umbellata), today largely commercial alizarin.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark notes alizarin is brought from Mumbai, and that madder and chay were historically the fine sources of red in the south. Ghosh states alizarin is now used instead of organic matter. A practitioner notes that powdered red-root dyes in trade are hard to identify as chay or madder.

concepts.summary: Indigo, from cakes, is printed directly (with rice starch rather than gum) since it needs no mordant; natural indigo has largely been replaced by synthetic blue.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark: indigo from indigo cakes, mixed with rice starch and not gum for printing; printed directly. Historically, chintz workers used wax resist and vat dipping for blue. Ghosh says natural indigo is no longer used and a lighter synthetic is used instead.

concepts.summary: Buffalo milk is used in the pre-treatment with myrobalan and added to the rice starch used for yellow, to prevent colours running.
concepts.body_md: Accounts differ on where it enters: with myrobalan before printing (journalism, Ghosh) or in the starch for yellow (Craftmark). A practitioner explains its fat as preventing dye spread.

concepts.summary: Dung-water soaking is the traditional bleaching / de-starching step for the grey cloth.
concepts.body_md: The grey cloth is soaked in dung and water, kept wet overnight, then washed in flowing water and sun-dried; Craftmark notes that today it may be dipped only once as cleansing rather than bleaching. The district page describes an alkaline scour instead.

concepts.summary: Natural gum thickens mordant and colour pastes for block printing and is washed out afterwards.
concepts.body_md: Mordants and most colours (except indigo) are mixed with gum for printing; washing in flowing water removes gum and unfixed mordant.

concepts.summary: Rice gruel starch, often with buffalo milk, is applied before the yellow stage to prevent diffusion and used as the indigo printing medium.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark describes cooking rice to a mass, straining, mixing with buffalo milk; starching prevents yellow from seeping to the reverse side.

concepts.summary: Leaves and flowers are added to the boiling bath — jajaku (gaja) leaves as carrier/fixer, moduga (palash) and anar/danimma (pomegranate) to shift reds toward orange or yellow.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark gives combinations: alizarin alone = red; + moduga = light orange; + anar = dark orange; moduga alone = yellowish-orange; myrobalan flowers alone = yellow. Sahapedia calls the forest leaves gaja and says they fix colours. News reporting adds pomegranate peel for mustard and roots/barks for brown.

concepts.summary: Beeswax is listed as a raw material and used as a resist before indigo in the wider Andhra kalamkari process.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark lists beeswax and broken pots for melting wax; Asia InCH describes wax resist with a kalam before indigo, removed by boiling. Its current use in Pedana printing is not confirmed by the sources.

concepts.summary: Hand-carved wooden (usually teak) blocks, one per colour, carry the outline, fill and background designs.
concepts.body_md: The design drawing is transferred onto teak blocks, each colour having its own block. Block makers cut blocks from the wood cross-section, unlike temple carvers who use longitudinal sections.

concepts.summary: A long low workbench covered with gunny and a damp cloth that stops the fabric slipping.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark gives dimensions of 63 × 27 × 18 inches so the printer can squat beside it.

concepts.summary: A teak tray with bamboo separators, a sponge layer and a woollen or gunny blotter that meters mordant onto the block.
concepts.body_md: The sponge holds a limited quantity of mordant; the woollen cloth acts as a blotter so only surface residue touches the block.

concepts.summary: Large vessels on brick fireplaces/ovens are used to boil mordant-printed cloth in the dye bath; sources disagree on copper vs iron vessels.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark and journalism describe copper pots; Sahapedia describes semi-circular iron vessels over ovens fuelled by rice husk and wood powder.

concepts.summary: A barrel-shaped stone (or mud) pot sunk almost entirely into the ground holds the fermenting iron liquor.
A date-palm-stick brush applies yellow by hand; the kalam (pen) is used for wax resist and fine details.
Designs are drawn on paper and carved into wooden blocks, one per colour.
concepts.body_md: Block making is the first listed stage in craft documentation and happens within or alongside the printing karkhana.

concepts.summary: The grey cloth is cleaned of starch and impurities by dung-water soaking and washing (traditional) or by boiling in an alkaline solution (current district description).
concepts.body_md: Craftmark: soak in dung water, keep wet overnight, wash in flowing water, spread over waterweed and sun-dry. District page: boil 2–3 hours in soda ash, caustic soda or detergent solution.

concepts.summary: The bleached cloth is dipped in myrobalan solution, squeezed and sun-dried, turning yellowish and becoming receptive to mordants.
Outlines and black areas are block-printed with gum-thickened kasim on the myrobalan-treated cloth.
concepts.body_md: Iron reacts with the tannin from the myrobalan treatment to produce black; this stage defines the design.

concepts.summary: Alum paste is block-printed on areas (and backgrounds) that are to turn red or pink.
concepts.body_md: Craftmark also states that the background is printed first, followed by outline and motifs — inconsistent with "iron precedes alum"; see open question.

concepts.summary: The printed cloth is left to dry for one to three days before washing.
The cloth is washed in flowing water to remove gum and unfixed mordant, then sun-dried.
concepts.body_md: Washing about an hour in flowing water prevents mordant from spreading into unwanted areas.

concepts.summary: The mordant-printed cloth is boiled about 1.5 hours in alizarin with jajaku leaves (and other plant additives for orange/yellow); red develops on alum areas and black is fixed.
After red develops the cloth is taken out, squeezed and dried in the sun.
concepts.body_md: Fact-check note: single-sourced (Craftmark, S4). The News Minute (S15) instead describes washing out residues after boiling; no second source explicitly describes squeezing and sun-drying at this point.

concepts.summary: After starching, yellow (myrobalan, brushed), green, grey and indigo are applied in a second round.
concepts.body_md: Indigo is printed directly without mordant; green is yellow plus indigo or from pomegranate.

concepts.summary: The cloth is submerged in a cool alum solution; excess yellow runs off and colours are fixed.
A short soap wash and sun-drying complete the cloth.
concepts.body_md: The whole sequence can take almost two months depending on weather (Craftmark).

concepts.summary: Printers reverse the order of background and motif printing depending on the colour: an indigo or indigo-green background is printed last.
The dyer controls shade through time in the bath and the choice of additives (moduga, anar, myrobalan flowers).
Different alum strengths printed on one cloth yield multiple shades from the same dye bath.
Mordant-printed cloth must be kept dry and allowed to cure before washing to stop mordants spreading.
Iron implements are kept away from alum preparations because any iron darkens the colour.
Progress depends on favourable weather for sun-drying and washing.
Motifs include ornamental birds, flowers, creepers, lotus, twines, mehrab/mihrab arches, the tree of life and cypress, reflecting Golconda/Persian taste.
Compositions are built in layers: a black (iron) outline block, alum fill/background blocks, then separate blocks for yellow, green, indigo.
The core palette is black, red, blue, yellow and green, extended to pinks, oranges and greys by additives and dilutions.
Designs have long been customised to buyers — Persian, European, Southeast Asian, and today overseas and fashion clients.
concepts.body_md: Ghosh records the designer Nelly Sethna reworking old Machilipatnam blocks in the 1970s and stopping the final bleaching to give an off-white ground.

concepts.summary: The process yields mordant-fixed, washable cotton textiles: sarees, dress material, bed covers, curtains, wall hangings, prayer cloths and canopies historically.
A single alizarin bath gives red on alum areas, deepens/fixes black on iron areas, and tints unmordanted areas pinkish.
Cheaper screen-printed "kalamkari" with chemical colours dominates the market and is hard to distinguish from block-printed work.
Tannin in myrobalan reacts with iron to give black, improves fastness of alum-red, and helps cotton take up iron and alum salts evenly.
Alum and iron mordants printed in different areas produce different colours (red vs black) when the whole cloth is boiled in a single red dye bath.
Indigo fixes without a mordant, so it is printed directly (Pedana) or applied by resist-and-dip (historical chintz).
Practitioners explain that milk fat penetrates the fibre and stops dyes spreading; not chemically verified in fetched sources.
Repeated washing in flowing water — at Machilipatnam the Kalia Canal, and ponds/canals around Pedana — removes gum, unfixed mordant and dung.
Sun-drying follows almost every wet stage, and spreading the bleached cloth in the sun is part of whitening; work depends on favourable weather.
Museum scholarship links the Coromandel Coast's chintz pre-eminence to local soil, water and dye plants.
Washing screen-printed, chemical-dyed cloth in canals and ponds is reported to pollute water, prompting official notices.
Srikalahasti kalamkari is freehand pen-painted, mainly temple narrative cloths made in family units; Machilipatnam is block-printed in karkhanas with Persian-derived motifs for trade.
concepts.body_md: Sources contrast the two: Srikalahasti uses tamarind-twig charcoal sketches and bamboo kalams, Hindu mythological themes and washing in the Swarnamukhi river; Machilipatnam uses teak blocks per colour, cross-cultural floral motifs and canal washing.

concepts.summary: Sahapedia states alum is not used for red at Machilipatnam, while the district government page and Craftmark describe alum (karam) printing as the red mordant.
Craftmark and journalism report copper pots; Sahapedia reports iron vessels — relevant because iron would dull alum reds.
Craftmark states iron printing precedes alum, yet also that the (alum) background is printed before the outline; actual order may vary by design.
Registry shows certificate 10-07-2008; secondary sources say 2012 or 2013 (possibly authorised-user registration).

Craftmark calls karakkaya "dried flowers" while Ghosh describes unripe fruit (and also yellow from dried flowers); sources place buffalo milk either with myrobalan pre-treatment or in the yellow starch.
concepts.body_md: Fact-check note: Ghosh's unripe-fruit statement appears in her paragraph on Kalahasti, not Machilipatnam.

concepts.summary: Estimates range from "minimum 10 steps" and days per piece to almost two months for the whole process.
Historical reds came from chay/madder; current Pedana practice appears to use commercial alizarin, but the share of natural vs synthetic dyes is not documented.
A GI-registered hand block-printed textile tradition of Sanganer town near Jaipur, known for fine repetitive floral motifs on a white ground.
concepts.body_md: The GI statement of case defines Sanganeri hand block printing as textiles printed only by stamping wooden hand blocks, with a white base colour, delicate floral motifs, repetitive designs and one or more colours that may overlap or circumscribe one another. The goods covered are dress material, home furnishings and garments (Classes 24 and 25). The registry lists it as GI application no. 147 (Handicraft, Rajasthan).

concepts.summary: Production is centred on Sanganer town, tehsil headquarters about 16 km from Jaipur, plus nearby villages.
concepts.body_md: The GI application defines the production area as Sanganer town, headquarters of Sanganer tehsil in Jaipur district, and nearby villages. It reported 315 printing units in Sanganer and more than twenty exporting units at the time of filing. A 2012 field study reported 473 units in eight clusters, a figure taken from a 2003 High Court sub-committee report.

concepts.summary: Sources attribute the town's founding to Sangaji, a Kachhwaha prince, in the early 16th century; a tourism source instead names Rana Sanga of Mewar.
concepts.body_md: The GI application, citing Hanuman Sharma and Chandramani Singh, states that Sanganer was founded by Sangaji, son of Prithviraj of Amber, in the early 16th century. Gaatha repeats the Kachhwaha prince attribution. The Incredible India portal instead says the town was established by Rana Sanga, a Mewar Rajput. See the open question on founding.

concepts.summary: Printing at Sanganer is linked to printers who migrated from Gujarat (and possibly Malwa) and to patronage by the Jaipur court, notably Sawai Jai Singh.
concepts.body_md: The GI application records the oral tradition, said to be confirmed by archival sources, that Sawai Jai Singh invited craftsmen to Jaipur, including printers from Gujarat, and conjectures that Malwa craftsmen also came. Impart describes the craft as widely believed to stem from mid-17th-century upheavals in Gujarat (Mughal and Maratha campaigns) that drove Kathiawar printers to Rajasthan, and treats Jai Singh patronage as conjecture. The V&A notes that Sanganer printing was established to serve, and encouraged by, the Jaipur court.

concepts.summary: Documentary evidence for printing at Sanganer begins in the early 18th century (tax records of 1703, rangkhana records of 1727), with dated pieces from 1799 onward.
concepts.body_md: The GI application notes that East India Company records of the 16th and 17th centuries do not mention Sanganer. Dastur-al-amal reports of 1703 describe taxes on printed fabrics, and rangkhana (royal dyeing and printing department) records of 1727 also refer to the trade. A City Palace head-dress bears an octroi seal dated V.S. 1856 (1799 CE). Several Sanganer-printed dupattas carry dated octroi stamps, including 1853 and 1906. A collection of sayings dated 1796 refers to the 'colours of Sanganer'.

concepts.summary: Sanganer cottons were known as chintz; examples were bought from the 1851 Great Exhibition and entered the V&A in the 1880s.
concepts.body_md: The V&A holds Sanganer block-printed cottons from about 1850, purchased from the Great Exhibition of 1851, and a chintz ('cheet') registered in 1883. The museum notes that British critics at the 1851 exhibition admired this type of 'flat' decoration. Jain and Hada report that Sanganer printed cloth was known as chintz in Europe. The Imperial Gazetteer (1908), quoted in the GI application, noted the industry was decaying because of machine competition.

concepts.summary: Printing at Sanganer is the hereditary work of the Chhipa community; the GI application says the skill is restricted to them.
concepts.body_md: The GI application states that the skill is limited to the Chhipas, who learned it from parents and grandparents, and that only skilled Chhipas know how to prepare colour mixtures in specific ratios. Jain and Hada describe the Chhipa printers as Hindus and followers of Sant Namdev. A 2025 interview study found Sanganer respondents mostly from the Khatri or Chhipa communities.

concepts.summary: Blocks are carved by turners known locally as Kharadis; carving numbers grew after migration from Farrukhabad in the 1970s.
concepts.body_md: The GI application credits the Kharadis (turners) with carving blocks from dried wood of shisham, gurjan, mango and teak, and names the steel chisels they use (kalam). Impart notes the carvers have been historically little documented: most carving was done in Sanganer until the 20th century, the number of carvers increased with migration from Farrukhabad in the 1970s, and 52 carving units were counted in 2008.

concepts.summary: Screen printing arrived around 1960 and spread widely; most production shifted to synthetic dyes, alongside a 1970s revival and a setback from the 1981 floods.
concepts.body_md: Jain and Hada report that screen printing came to Sanganer around 1960, taken up by Khatri printers who had migrated from Mirpur and Sind, and that many families shifted to mill cloth, synthetic dyes and screens. They describe a 1970s revival under Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay, Pupul Jayakar, Laila Tyabji and Anokhi, a setback from floods in 1981, and a UNIDO cluster programme in 1997. The GI application says screen-printed imitations sold as 'Sanganeri' were a main reason for seeking GI protection. Gaatha dates chemical dyes to the 1980s.

concepts.summary: GI application no. 147 was registered in the 2009-10 registry year; a 2025 study found Sanganer artisans rarely use the GI in marketing.
concepts.body_md: The GI Registry lists application 147 within the April 2009 to March 2010 section. The GI application proposed an inspection body and a CPCSL-issued wooden seal to be stamped on finished goods. A 2025 interview study found half of Sanganer respondents aware of the GI and 96.9% not using it in marketing.

concepts.summary: Mostly cotton, especially fine mulmul, sometimes cotton-silk or silk; today a wider range of fibres is used.
concepts.body_md: The GI description says Sanganeri textiles are mostly on cotton and sometimes on cotton-silk; the safa (turban) is printed on fine 'mulmul'. The GI materials section accepts all natural fabrics and man-made fibres such as rayon and poly-cotton. Jain and Hada report that a decade before their study mostly mulmul cotton was used, with silk reserved for royalty, while crepe, georgette, linen, khadi and jute are now also printed.

concepts.summary: Powdered myrobalan (Terminalia chebula), a tannin source, used to pre-treat the cloth so it takes mordants and turns black with iron.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes harda powder mixed with water as a tannic-acid pre-treatment that attracts the block-printed mordants and forms black with the iron mordant. It gives the cloth a creamish-yellow tint, hence the name 'pila karna'. Gaatha calls it the link between the fibres and the other ingredients.

concepts.summary: A fermented solution of iron from rusted horseshoes or scrap iron with jaggery and gum, printed as the black outline.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes syahi as a fermented solution of iron with molasses (jaggery, gur) and gum, made from rusted horseshoe nails, which develops a deep black with harda. Gaatha describes it as scrap iron, horseshoes and gur prepared in an earthenware vessel. Jain and Hada report the iron and jaggery steeped in cold water for about a fortnight in a closed mud pot.

concepts.summary: An alum paste thickened with tree gum and tinted with geru (red ochre), printed where red is wanted.
concepts.body_md: In the GI application, begar paste is the alum mordant that develops a rich red with alizarin. Gaatha describes begar as alum mixed with sticky tree gum and a pinch of geru. Jain and Hada describe the red ('beggar') made with alum and geru, a red soil.

concepts.summary: The red dye bath, historically madder (Rubia spp.), now mostly synthetic alizarin, which gives red on alum and black on iron.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes the alizarine bath as prepared from madder (Rubia tinctorum, Rubia manjista), containing alizarin and purpurin, and notes that synthetic alizarin is now used because of a shortage of the vegetable dye. The V&A identifies madder red on a Sanganer cotton of about 1850.

concepts.summary: Flowers of the dhawai shrub (Woodfordia) boiled with alizarin, reportedly to avoid patches and staining.
concepts.body_md: The GI application says 'dhawai ka phool' (Woodfordia, given as 'Fordia floribunda') is mixed with alizarine in specific ratios, and that a local flower boiled with the alizarin prevents patches and staining. Gaatha names 'dhaura ka phool' together with a few drops of castor or sesame oil in the red dyeing.

concepts.summary: A resist paste of black clay (kali mitti), lime, wheat flour and gum, made to family recipes, used to reserve areas from indigo.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes dabu as a clay-lime-gum-wheat paste ('insect-eaten wheat' is mentioned) and lists the ingredients as kali mitti, lime (bidhan), wheat flour and gum mixed in ratios that depend on the type of dabu needed. Each family keeps its own recipe secret.

concepts.summary: Sprinkled over freshly printed dabu to absorb water and add an extra resist layer.
concepts.body_md: According to the GI application, sawdust is sprinkled on freshly block-printed dabu; it absorbs water from the paste and gives additional layers of resist.

concepts.summary: Blue from Indigofera tinctoria, now usually synthetic indigo granules, used in a vat kept alive with lime and jaggery.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes indigo as blue colouring matter from nil plants (Indigofera tinctoria), now usually replaced by synthetic indigo granules. The vat is kept alive by adding indigo, lime and jaggery.

concepts.summary: A fugitive yellow from turmeric (haldi) and pomegranate rind (naspal), fixed afterwards with alum; over indigo it gives green.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes a yellow dye extracted from haldi and naspal that is very fugitive and must be fixed by post-mordanting with alum. The V&A attributes green on a Sanganer cotton of about 1850 to indigo overdyed with a yellow, probably turmeric.

concepts.summary: Aluminium salt used as the red mordant in begar and as a dilute post-mordant to fix the yellow.
concepts.body_md: The GI application names aluminium sulphate as one of the two printed mordants and describes a dilute alum (fitkari) bath to fix the turmeric and pomegranate yellow.

concepts.summary: Used traditionally for scouring and as a mild alkaline solution sprinkled during sun-bleaching.
concepts.body_md: The GI application records that cow dung was traditionally used to scour the cloth, now largely replaced by soaps. A mild cow-dung solution is also sprinkled on fabric during sun-bleaching (tapai).

concepts.summary: Most present-day Sanganer printing uses synthetic dyes (rapid, indigosol, pigments, azo-free dyes); natural dyes are used mainly to order.
concepts.body_md: The GI application lists natural and/or synthetic (azo-free) dyes. Jain and Hada report a trade association estimate that 95% of dyes used in the area were synthetic, with rapid and indigosol dyes and pigments common, and metallic and glitter pigments added. Kathju and Kashyap report heavy use of chemical dyes in Sanganer, with natural dyes kept for specific orders.

concepts.summary: Hand-carved hardwood blocks with a handle, made in many shapes; separate blocks are carved for outline, fill and background.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes buntas as wooden blocks in rectangular, square, circular, oval and segmental shapes; the quarter-circle segmental block is called 'chand'. A wooden handle is fixed on top, which the printer holds and strikes. Woods named are shisham, gurjan, mango and teak. The V&A says the blocks must be very hard wood, usually teak, and that the most esteemed blocks come from Pethapur in Gujarat. It calls Sanganer blocks chhapas or buntis.

concepts.summary: Each colour needs its own block: rekh for the outline, datta or datai for fills, and optionally a second outline or background block.
concepts.body_md: The GI application names the block types as rekh (outline), datta (filler) and background blocks. Jain and Hada list rekh (outline), chirai (second outline, if required) and datai (fill), with as many blocks as there are colours. Gaatha describes begar applied with a datta block to fill the rekh.

concepts.summary: Cloth is stretched on a low bench or long table covered with several layers of heavy cloth padding.
concepts.body_md: The GI application, quoting Ritu Kumar, describes a low bench covered with a thick pad of several layers of heavy cloth, with the printer squatting before it. It names two kinds of table: a low 'patia' and a long printing table. Impart describes printing on a long table.

concepts.summary: A shallow tray holding a frame and layers of jute and cotton cloth saturated with colour, which inks the block evenly.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes small rectangular colour containers with a frame and layers of jute and cotton inside that spread the colour evenly and form a pad. A separate pan is prepared for each colour, and a trolley moves the colour mixtures.

concepts.summary: Steel chisels of different widths and cutting edges used by Kharadis to engrave blocks.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes kalams as steel chisels of different widths and cutting surfaces used by the block-makers to engrave motifs on printing blocks.

concepts.summary: Large copper vessels heated by wood fire (bhatti) hold the alizarin bath and the alum post-mordant bath.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes alizarin dyeing in large copper vessels heated by wood fire, with the dye placed in small cloth bags. Gaatha names the copper vessel 'tamda' and the furnace 'bhatti'.

concepts.summary: A wooden mallet used to beat harda-treated cloth and the folds of moist finished cloth.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes the mogri as a wooden mallet used to beat the folds of moist finished cloth. In the harda stage, dried cloth is folded and beaten with a wooden mallet to remove excess powder.

concepts.summary: A fermentation vat that is hard to start but kept 'alive' indefinitely by replenishment.
concepts.body_md: The GI application says starting a new indigo tank is tedious and complicated, but once ready it is kept alive by constant additions of indigo, lime and jaggery.

concepts.summary: Kharadis smooth the wood, transfer the design, carve, level the ground, trim the sides and fit a handle.
concepts.body_md: Jain and Hada describe a carving sequence: ghisai (smoothing the block), chakai (transferring the design from tracing paper onto a surface coated with titanium dioxide and adhesive), khudai (carving, 2-3 mm up to 2 inches), dabana (levelling the background), chilai (smoothing the sides so repeats match) and fitting the hatha (handle). This is a preparatory craft, separate from the 12-step cloth sequence.

concepts.summary: Mill or handloom cloth is cleaned of starch, oil and dust, traditionally with cow dung and repeated wetting in the sun over 3-6 days.
concepts.body_md: Per the GI application, cloth is now boiled with soap and desizing agents. Traditionally it was left overnight in cow dung and water, then spread on open ground and re-wetted 5-6 times a day until white and bright, taking 3 to 6 days, before a wash in clean water. Gaatha calls this rigorous scouring 'teluni'.

concepts.summary: Cloth is soaked in harda solution, squeezed, dried flat, then folded and beaten.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes submerging the cloth in harda and water, squeezing it and drying it flat on the ground. The dry cloth is folded and beaten with a wooden mallet to remove excess powder and open the fibre. The yellowish result gives the name 'peela karna'.

concepts.summary: Syahi (iron) is printed with outline blocks and begar (alum) with filler blocks, one tray per colour.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes inking the block on a dye-saturated pad and stamping it onto cloth on a padded table. The cloth is printed with two mordants: ferrous syahi, usually with the outline block, and aluminium begar with the filler block. Gaatha says the cloth then dries for a week.

concepts.summary: Printed cloth is left at least 3-4 days so the mordant paste penetrates the fibre.
concepts.body_md: The GI application states the printed fabric is left for at least three to four days so the mordant paste penetrates the fibre, and that longer ageing gives better results.

concepts.summary: Aged cloth is washed in running water to remove excess mordant and gum before dyeing.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes washing the printed fabric in running water to remove excess mordant before dyeing. Gaatha describes a thorough wash to remove the tree gum.

concepts.summary: The mordanted cloth is boiled with alizarin and dhawai flowers in copper vessels for about half a day, giving red on alum and black on iron.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes dyeing in large wood-fired copper vessels, with alizarin in small cloth bags and dhawai flowers added to prevent patches. Dyeing usually takes half a day, after which the cloth is dried on the ground. One dye reacts with two mordants to give two colours.

concepts.summary: The dyed cloth is laid on a river bed and repeatedly sprinkled with dilute cow dung to restore a white ground; the GI calls this the most typical Sanganer step.
concepts.body_md: The GI application explains that alizarin over-dyes the unprinted ground to an off-white or yellow tinge, so the fabric is laid flat on a river bed and sprinkled with a mild cow dung solution, again as it dries. It calls tapai the most typical part of Sanganeri production and unique to it. Gaatha describes washing in running river water and drying in scorching sun with periodic sprinkling to obtain a white ground.

concepts.summary: Dabu paste is block-printed over areas to keep from indigo, dusted with sawdust and sun-dried.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes dabu as a mechanical resist block-printed onto the fabric and covered with sawdust. The fabric is then sun-dried before indigo dipping. Because the paste is thick and sticky, sharp definition is not achieved. It is used only for indigo patterns.

concepts.summary: Pleated cloth is lowered into the vat, opened under the liquor, lifted to oxidise, and re-dipped until the shade is reached.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes folding the cloth like sari pleats, lowering it gently into the tank and opening each pleat under the liquid so dye reaches it evenly. The cloth is squeezed and opened to air to oxidise. The first dip gives pale sky blue, and dipping is repeated for darker blues. Before the yellow stage, dabu is printed again to keep some areas blue.

concepts.summary: With dabu re-applied, four people hold the cloth while a fifth rubs turmeric-pomegranate dye on with loose woollen cloth.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes printing dabu again, taking the fabric to an open area where four people hold the corners, and a fifth person mopping on the turmeric and pomegranate dye with loose-woven woollen cloth that holds enough dye. The work is done gently so the dabu stays on.

concepts.summary: The yellowed cloth is dipped briefly in dilute alum, dried, and stored folded in the dark for 3-4 days so the yellow sets.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes dipping the fabric for a few minutes in a copper vessel of water with diluted alum, squeezing it gently and drying it flat. When fully dry it is folded and stored in a dark place for at least 3 to 4 days so the yellow sets.

concepts.summary: Cloth is soaked 3-4 hours to soften the resist, then beaten on stone slabs in flowing water to remove dabu and loose dye.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes leaving the fabric in large tanks for at least 3 to 4 hours until the resist paste softens, then beating it on a flat stone slab, usually where water flows, to remove the paste and excess dye.

concepts.summary: Printers usually lay the black outline first because it shows immediately and guides the filler block; sometimes the background block goes first.
concepts.body_md: The GI application explains that the iron outline is usually printed first because it leaves an immediately visible black impression, which makes it easy for another printer to place the filler block. It adds that the background block is sometimes applied before the outline. Jain and Hada stress even spacing and equal pressure across repeated impressions.

concepts.summary: Experienced dyers judge alizarin quantity; colour and dabu mixtures follow family-held ratios rather than written recipes.
concepts.body_md: The GI application states that the experienced dyer calculates the quantity of alizarin, that colour mixtures are prepared in specific ratios by skilled Chhipas, and that each family keeps its own secret dabu recipe, with ratios varied by the type of dabu needed.

concepts.summary: The indigo dyer judges the vat by its colour and adds ingredients by experience, with no written recipe.
concepts.body_md: According to the GI application, an expert indigo dyer can tell the state of the vat from its colour and adds the exact quantity of each ingredient learned from experience. There is no written recipe, and every family handles indigo its own way.

concepts.summary: Dyers unfold pleats under the liquor to avoid trapped air and move gently so the dabu does not crack or wash off; alum baths are kept short.
concepts.body_md: The GI application notes that air trapped in folds gives patchy dyeing, so pleats are opened under the liquid, gently, so the dabu does not crack. Yellow is mopped on gently so the dabu does not come off, and the alum dip is limited to a few minutes because a long dip makes the dabu come off.

concepts.summary: Printers leave mordant prints at least 3-4 days (Gaatha reports about a week), on the rule that longer ageing gives better results.
concepts.body_md: The GI application sets a minimum of three to four days of ageing and says longer is better. Gaatha reports drying for a week after begar printing.

concepts.summary: Designs were chosen to suit the community, occasion and patron; today buyers often dictate motif and placement.
concepts.body_md: Ritu Kumar, quoted in the GI application, says Sanganer motifs had to suit the occasion, location and requirements of the patrons. Kamlesh Mathur, also quoted there, says the gentry preferred dark yellow, green and pink with natural floral designs, while local people preferred red and black. Jain and Hada report that buyers now decide motif and pattern and that placement is designed for garment construction.

concepts.summary: Designs are described as buti (small motif), buta (larger single motif), jhar/jaal (bunch or net) and bel (border).
concepts.body_md: The GI application says design forms are known by one or more of buti, buta, jhar and border, and that every Sanganeri textile carries buti, buta or jhar or combinations of them. Jain and Hada define buti as a very small motif at predetermined spacing (up to 20 on a block), buta as a single complete motif usually no larger than 3 x 5 inches, jaal as a continuous interconnected all-over pattern (less common in Sanganer), and bel as 2-4 inch borders. Impart calls the small patterns 'bhant' and reports over four hundred types.

concepts.summary: Delicate, finely lined, highly stylised flowers, buds and leaves repeated at measured intervals on a white ground.
concepts.body_md: The GI application lists motif sources as flowers, leaves and buds, intertwisted tendrils, figurative and geometric designs, with more than a hundred traditional designs. Saris use lotus, iris, rose, poppy, water lily, narcissus, marigold, sunflower and similar flowers, composed into mango, betel-leaf, dagger and jhumka shapes. The V&A dates the orderly offset rows of florals to 17th-century Mughal court designs. Impart links iris, tulip and narcissus, flowers not grown locally, to Mughal influence and the cabbage rose to East India Company trade.

concepts.summary: A single piece combines several designs, such as buti in the field, bel on edges and buta on the end panel, in harmony.
concepts.body_md: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay, quoted in the GI application and by Jain and Hada, describes a variety of designs harmonised in the same cloth as a special feature of Sanganer prints. Jain and Hada describe sari planning with buti in the body, bel on the edges and buta on the end panel, needing many blocks. Butis from two blocks can be printed together to make a third (e.g. singhbal buti).

concepts.summary: Red-and-black syahi-begar for local men's safas, soft florals for the Jaipur court, red on white or yellow for temple cloths, bandhani-imitating veils for women.
concepts.body_md: Gaatha and Impart describe syahi-begar (black and red on white) for safas and angochhas worn by local men, florals on white or soft grounds for Jaipur court society, and red on white or yellow for temple dupattas and shawls. Impart adds bandhani-imitating designs for women, such as the mali chunnari and mina chaddar. The GI application describes safas with white ground, black outline and red, and Shiva-worship dupattas with damaru, trident and dhatura motifs.

concepts.summary: The finished cloth shows red and black (plus blue, yellow and green when used) on a white ground restored by sun-bleaching.
concepts.body_md: The GI application gives white as the base colour and says saris are mainly red and black with shades of yellow, brown, indigo blue and green. Gaatha reports that river washing and sun drying give a white background and clear, rich colours. V&A pieces from about 1850 show red and green or indigo and madder florals on white.

concepts.summary: The GI application specifies that the design shows almost as vividly on the underside.
concepts.body_md: The GI specification and uniqueness statement say the design is equally vividly seen on the underside of the cloth. Jain and Hada attribute this to the precision of the wooden-block impressions.

concepts.summary: Sanganer was historically known for bright, fast dyes, cited as its main contribution to Indian printing.
concepts.body_md: The GI application cites Jaipur State records and a 1796 collection of sayings referring to the 'colours of Sanganer', and Ritu Kumar's view that the main contributions of Sanganer printers were fast colours and well-proportioned lyrical motifs.

concepts.summary: Green areas come from yellow applied over indigo-dyed areas, with dabu keeping some areas blue.
concepts.body_md: The GI application says the fabric goes to yellow dyeing to turn it green, with dabu reprinted first to keep some blue. The V&A identifies green on a Sanganer piece as indigo plus a yellow, probably turmeric.

concepts.summary: Saris, chintz yardage for ghagharas, suits and dupattas, safas and home furnishings.
concepts.body_md: The GI application lists saris, chintz (chheent) yardage for skirts (ghagharas), salwar suits with dupattas, safas about 8 m by 0.9 m, and home furnishings such as bedspreads, quilts, cushion covers and curtains. Jain and Hada note that menswear is now printed too, which it was not earlier.

concepts.summary: Source-stated mechanism: in one alizarin bath, alum-printed areas turn red and iron-printed areas turn black.
concepts.body_md: The GI application states that dyeing is a reaction of the dye with two mordants at two locations on the same print, giving red with alum and black with iron. It also notes that the iron syahi forms black with the tannic acid of harda. These source statements are linked to the shared mechanism concepts for alum complexation, alizarin lake formation, iron-tannin black and tannin pre-mordanting.

concepts.summary: The GI application attributes the whitening in tapai to the alkali of cow dung combined with heat from sunlight.
concepts.body_md: According to the GI application, the interaction of the alkali in cow dung with thermal heat from the sun bleaches the over-dyed ground back to white. This is the applicant's explanation; the detailed photochemistry is left to the shared sun-bleaching mechanism concept.

concepts.summary: Dabu physically blocks indigo from reaching covered fibre; sawdust absorbs moisture and thickens the barrier.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes dabu as a mechanical resist that prevents dye from penetrating covered areas, with sawdust absorbing water from the paste and adding resist layers.

concepts.summary: The GI application explains that reduced indigo turns blue on contact with air and that depth is built through repeated dips.
concepts.body_md: The GI application states that fabric lifted from the vat reacts with atmospheric oxygen, turning reduced indigo into oxidised indigo. Indigo has poor affinity for the fabric, so the first dip is pale and repeated dips build darker shades. It also explains that trapped air in pleats causes patchiness.

concepts.summary: Running water and riverbanks were central to washing and bleaching; sources name the river differently.
concepts.body_md: Gaatha reports that chhipa families moved to places with space and running water near Jaipur, and that Sanganer's riverbanks suited dyers and bleachers. The GI application describes sun-bleaching on a river bed and final washing where water flows. Impart names the river Dhoondh. Jain and Hada and the Incredible India portal attribute the character of the shades to the water of the 'Saraswati'. India Water Portal says the nallahs now drain to the Dravyawati river.

concepts.summary: Low rainfall (about 556 mm/yr) and strong sun allow open-air drying, ageing and sun-bleaching on open grounds.
concepts.body_md: The GI application gives an annual rainfall of 556 mm and temperatures of 3 to 50 °C, and claims Sanganer still has geographical and climatic conditions conducive to the desired shades and fine designs. Several steps depend on sun and open ground: scouring on open grounds, drying flat on the ground after harda and dyeing, sun-drying dabu, and tapai.

concepts.summary: Untreated dyeing and printing wastewater from Sanganer units pollutes the Amanishah Nallah and local groundwater.
concepts.body_md: Husain et al. (2013) found the units' wastewater high in sodium, chloride and sulfate, with copper, chromium and iron. It was discharged untreated into the Amanishah Nallah, and eleven groundwater samples were polluted by percolation. India Water Portal (2015) reports 12.3 MLD officially and 17-18 MLD estimated untreated discharge, and describes a long dispute over a Common Effluent Treatment Plant. The GI application reports 1-2 m³/day effluent for small units and a planned CETP. Jain and Hada attribute much of the pollution to screen-printing units.

concepts.summary: Estimates range from the 16th to the 18th century, and from '500 years' to about 250-300 years.
concepts.body_md:
The town is dated to the early 16th century, but documentary evidence for printing starts with 1703 and 1727 records. The GI application concludes printing is attested 'since as late as' the 18th century while claiming over 300 years of use. Impart and Gaatha favour a mid-17th-century migration. Incredible India and AIACA say the late 16th to early 17th century. NABARD calls the textiles about 500 years old, while Singh et al. (quoted) say at least 250 years.

Fact-check note (2026-10-14): Jain and Hada (S10), after noting the absence of pre-18th-century records, nonetheless conclude from Fostat fragments and European chintz that printing at Sanganer existed much earlier; this inference is not specific to Sanganer.

concepts.summary: The GI application and Gaatha name the Kachhwaha prince Sangaji; a tourism portal names Rana Sanga of Mewar.
concepts.body_md: Primary-leaning sources (the GI application citing Hanuman Sharma, and Gaatha) attribute the town to Sangaji, son of Prithviraj of Amber. The Incredible India portal says Rana Sanga of Mewar. The latter is low-reliability and uncorroborated in the sources read.

concepts.summary: The registry places application 147 in the April 2009-March 2010 year; secondary sources say 2009, 2010 or (wrongly) 2023.
concepts.body_md: The IP India list places the entry under April 2009 to March 2010 without a date. NABARD and Kathju and Kashyap say 2009. Impart, Jain and Hada, Incredible India and Wikipedia say 2010. AIACA says 2023, which conflicts with the registry. The certificate date was not found in an accessible GI Journal or registry page.

concepts.summary: Sources name the Dhoondh, the 'Saraswati' or the Dravyavati/Amanishah, and attribute the shades to local water without chemical evidence.
concepts.body_md: Impart names the Dhoondh. Jain and Hada and Incredible India name the 'Saraswati' and credit its water with the shades and radiance. India Water Portal names the Dravyawati as the receiving river of today's nallahs. None of the sources read gives water-chemistry evidence for a colour effect, so the claim remains untested.

concepts.summary: The GI method describes natural-dye steps, but field studies report about 95% synthetic dyes and 'natural' labels based on the gum used.
concepts.body_md: The GI application describes a traditional natural-dye process but also allows synthetic alizarin, synthetic indigo and azo-free synthetic dyes. Jain and Hada cite a 95% synthetic estimate and report that the trade labels prints 'natural' or 'chemical' by whether guar or synthetic gum is used, not by dye origin. Kathju and Kashyap report natural dyes only for specific orders. No independent measurement of the share was found.

concepts.summary: Studies measure pollution from 'dyeing and printing units' collectively; sources blame screen printing and disagree on discharge volumes and CETP status.
concepts.body_md: Husain et al. treat dyeing and printing units together. Jain and Hada describe screen-printing units as the main source. Discharge estimates differ (12.3 vs 17-18 MLD), and the GI application's planned CETP had not been built as of 2015 according to India Water Portal. The share attributable to hand block printing, and to natural vs synthetic processes, is not established in the sources read.
